descriptionText:
There are going to be many things you’ll have to balance to succeed, and it all has to be done concurrently. You can’t just work on one thing at a time, even though the main thing to overcome is a bottleneck, you must balance your personal productivity and work on several things at once. Today we will discuss: 

How to balance your personal productivity and ability to get things done and the effect it will have on overall success

Feeling overwhelmed, what it is, what it feels like, and how to adapt to it

Creating an ideal weekly routine

Routine and how it affects the feeling of overwhelm

post.title: Interview Prep Plan
post.content:
Hi Guys so randomly today I ended up getting scheduled from 3 different companies and it feels a bit overwhelming because they are within the next week or two and I am a bit over whelmed on how to prepare. I got to the final round for Capital One's TDP which is a 4 hour interview in one day. I got to a technical interview that is one hour for SoFi. And I got a response to talk with a recruiter for a company called Skillz, so it's just the first step so not too bad yet.

I am waiting on dates to be scheduled but based on dates they gave:
Sofi could be next week be any day Monday-Wednesday
C1 is probably one day from the 15-17th
Skillz is within the next week but just a call with recruiter

I am thinking of either
[ol:1][li]Grind Leetcode tagged of Sofi, then C1, then Skillz as it comes[li]Do Sofi and C1 at same time so I get more time for C1[li]Just do general Neetcode to get overall skill better for both

For C1 this is final round but for Sofi it has another round after and obviously Skillz will have more rounds but I don't know them yet

LeetCode Requirements

Please work through the Pareto Problem Set over the next 2 months. Most people complete 5-7 problems/week evenly. You'll also have access to LeetCode Office Hours weekly with our coding interview coache!

How To Access LeetCode Office Hours

Anytime you need help on DS&A, LeetCode problems, etc. please join a Technical Office Hours call with Henry. It's in the Calendar! This is separate to booking your mock coding interviews which is at the link in the Coaching Call Guide.

Hey everyone, based on student feedback I am updating my OH to be 1.5 hours each starting the week of February 23rd:
[ul][li][Launchpad OH: Mondays 6:00-7:30pm EST](https://us06web.zoom.us/meeting/register/FTQyvPxlR6ief7IjtlGQoQ)[li][Accelerator OH: Mondays 7:30pm-9:00pm EST](https://us06web.zoom.us/meeting/register/2IevHU9SSfyKtB1uXMDDow)

This should have a pretty wide coverage for people in different timezones.

This past Saturday we had an awesome session covering DP problems: Fibonacci, Factorial, Climbing Stairs, Coin Change, Longest Increasing Subsequence, Unique Paths. Please watch the recordings [here](https://us06web.zoom.us/rec/share/nm_3u4HjS4eLhHTgp6bMpu6S2F5sJ1lP5sZgKQltu8g0h_4q4iKB4Yt4ny8ju6N4.AzJhFbc5oGZxCfsW?startTime=1771088861000) \(Password: *t*.U8#Y\) - sorry I didn't make the password :\)

I've attached the notes below. If you are interested in more, let us know - we can cover more niche topics or anything you want to see.

Again thanks for the feedback and excited to make the Accelerator work best for you.
~Peter

post.title: 🚨 Need Help Booking Flex, Mock, or OH? Start Here
post.content:
We’ve been receiving a number of inquiries about how to book mock interviews, flex sessions, or join group Office Hours \(OH\) — we hear you!

To make things clearer, we’ve updated the Coaching Call Guide Module to make the scheduling process much more intuitive.

Please review the updated guide here: [https://www.skool.com/software-eng-accelerator/classroom/fe6af36c?md=e202d03341cc4c3080bd6833d2879cb5](https://www.skool.com/software-eng-accelerator/classroom/fe6af36c?md=e202d03341cc4c3080bd6833d2879cb5)

⚠️ Quick reminder on your coaching call eligibility:
🚀 For the 2-Month Intensive:
[ul][li]Mock Behavioral Interviews: 4[li]Mock Technical Interviews: 4[li]Flex Sessions: 4[li]Office Hours \(OH\): Minimum of 4
This completes the 16 coaching call requirement during your intensive period.

🚀 For Accelerator Core members \(1-month intensive\):
[ul][li]Your requirement is half of the sessions listed above.

⚠️ Important reminder: You are no longer eligible to sign up for mock interviews once your intensive period has ended, so please make sure to schedule and complete them within your program timeline.

Planning ahead will help ensure you complete all required sessions on time. If you have questions after reviewing the guide, feel free to reach out!

post.title: 🚀 Meet Our New Interview Coach — Brian Liu
post.content:
Hey everyone, I'm thrilled to introduce the latest addition to the Accelerator coaching team — and honestly, his offer list speaks for itself!

👨‍💻 [@Brian Liu](obj://user/9d95b9af470541fcae2a4b8afe0191e7) — Software Engineer & Technical Interview Coach

✅ Full-time new grad offers from Amazon, TikTok, Palantir, Databricks & Google
✅ Deep expertise in mock technical interviews & problem-solving strategy
✅ Knows firsthand what it takes to crack the most competitive hiring processes in tech

Brian didn't just land one dream offer — he landed five. He's been through the gauntlet at some of the most selective companies in the industry and is now here to pass that knowledge directly to you. Whether it's sharpening your LeetCode approach, building a stronger problem-solving framework, or simulating real interview pressure, Brian has been in your shoes and knows exactly what interviewers are looking for.

What This Means for You:
You now have a coach who's literally 5-for-5 on elite tech offers ready to help you refine your approach, level up your thinking, and walk into your next interview with confidence. If you've got a technical interview on the horizon, schedule a mock with Brian or tag him in the community for feedback on your prep!

Let's stack those offers 💪

— Aman

post.title: Officially into Google's team match phase
post.content:
Hi all, Have been grinding in this job search for a while now. After 8 months from the date of application, I have officially entered Google's team match phase.

To all the coaches, I just want to say thank you for everything you did till now right from helping me make my resume better to mock interviewing me with extremely useful feedback. And to Scott Novak, who understood my financial constraints and was extremely supportive. And special shoutout to [@Makan Azarshahy](obj://user/08e236c02af544998c2265f631a4cfcc) who honed me and made me 'Google Ready'.

I am still one coffee chat away from an official offer but for now I think I definitely deserve to celebrate this win.

Thanks again and good luck to everyone in this community. Rooting for you guys to get your wins very soon.

post.title: Resume Template
post.content:
Hey everyone,

A few of you reached out to me regarding my resume template, so here it is!

I made this into a .txt format doc so you can just copy and paste this into [www.overleaf.com](www.overleaf.com).

In a resume, experience \(substance\) is the most important, but formatting is often overlooked. I've used my resume everywhere I've applied, and so have my mentees in the past. We've seen tremendous results and think you can benefit as well. Main things here are to give you a clean format without overcluttering, but also let ATS/people's eyes pick up your most important accomplishments. I would say the icons are not needed but they are a nice addition.

If you have any questions, feel free to comment below!

~Peter

post.title: Got an Offer at PlayStation
post.content:
The title pretty much. I got an internship offer at PLAYSTATION! For summer 2026. I swear on my life 4 months ago had you told me I would’ve gotten into PlayStation, I would’ve told you you’re sick in the head. But after going through my first quarter of Masters at UC Irvine and 4 months through this program I feel on top of the world. You CAN do it. If you’re genuinely willing to put in the work, you can and will be rewarded in the long term. Do the practice, mock interviews, rehearse yourself, leetcode, all the necessary steps and you will succeed. Consistency compounds.

I genuinely can’t believe I got this offer, it’s within San Diego where I’m from too so couldn’t have been better.

I also personally want to give a huge thank you to Yvonne, Jon, and Peter for all the interview/coding tips. I couldn’t have done it without all of your advice. Yvonne with all your niche interview questions, Jon with the conversational tips, and Peter with the C++ extensive practice study guide. And of course to Aman and everyone else in this program who helped remind me of my goals.

descriptionText:
You apply. You message. Maybe you even get an interview…Then—silence. Or worse, a vague rejection. So what’s really going on?

In this eye-opening session, Jon and Yvonne pull back the curtain on the invisible API that connects job seekers and recruiters. This isn't your typical job search advice—it's a behind-the-scenes look at how recruiters actually work and how you can align your approach to stand out.

📌 In this session, you'll learn:

What recruiters really do day-to-day

How they source, screen, and select candidates

Why some outreach gets a response—and some disappears into the void

How to craft messages that actually get noticed

Tactical ways to prepare, position yourself, and build recruiter relationships that matter

Whether you're prepping for recruiting season or just trying to make sense of the hiring process, this talk will help you connect the dots and gain confidence in your next move.

📅 Originally Recorded: June 13, 2025 @ 1:00pm PT / 4:00pm ET

post.title: I created a Claude Code skill to get LinkedIn Connections
post.content:
Hey everyone, it's been a while since I've been here.

Once I got a job as a software engineer and I kind of just stopped looking at Skool. Sorry about that.

However, I've been back on the hunt and I've been trying to grow my LinkedIn connections.

I actually created a Claude Code workflow that navigates LinkedIn and automatically sends connection requests \(with notes\) to people at your school.

I've been using it for about two weeks and I've gained about a hundred connections in that time. Almost all of those connections are actively working software engineers.

It's extremely useful, obviously slower than humans, but it works in the background and it's easy to start. So let me know if this is something you guys would be interested in me posting.

The [skill.md](http://skill.md) file is attached.

****** PLEASE READ BEFORE USING ********

LinkedIn does not like bots.
Don't do more than 50 connections per day.
There are some things in this skill that purposely force synchronous actions DO NOT REMOVE THEM.
The skill prevents having +2 tabs going at a single time.
This is done on purpose. It prevents lag and prevents you getting banned.
If you do have multiple agents working in parallel you could very easily get banned.

**** You've been warned. Use it at your own risk ****

I've been using it for 2 weeks now with no issues \(30 connections / day\).
If I do have an issue I will let you know.

Change this skill to fit your needs and setup.

My skill uses Obsidian CLI + Skill and Playwright CLI + Skill.

I would recommend using these tools but it's up to you.

post.title: 🚀 The Power of the Second Ask: Overcoming Job Search Shame
post.content:
Before joining the Accelerator, I had a great opportunity: a referral from my very successful cousin, who works at Microsoft, for a Software Engineering role.

To my shock, Microsoft still ghosted even with the referral.

The shame was real. Based on the incredible \(and necessary\) constructive criticism I’ve received here, I know now that my resume simply wasn't reflecting my true value. But at the time, all I felt was the fear of disappointing my cousin. I was convinced he would be embarrassed that Microsoft didn't even respond to his referral.

It took overcoming that shame and discomfort—something the accelerator explicitly forced me to do—to try again. I cooked up the courage to reach out to him and ask for a referral once more, and his response was everything: he told me he would refer me "70x7 times"!

This is my reminder to everyone here: There is no shame in being rejected, ghosted, or needing to re-apply. Our field is competitive, and sometimes the only thing standing between you and the job is a more optimized resume or a better approach.

Don't let one failure prevent you from making the second ask. Get back up, refine your materials, and try once more. Your network is there to support your effort, not condemn your setbacks.

post.title: I won JP Morgans’s Code For Good
post.content:
Hey everyone just wanted to share a recent win i’m extremely proud of.

Over the course of this weekend I competed in one of the most competitive hackathons in the nation, with students flying in from California, New York, Texas, Florida, and Washington to name a few.

The networking opportunities at the event alone was a major win, but my team and I built software over the course of 24 hours for a non profit organization and ended up winning the competition.

The competition is a direct pipeline to JP Morgans summer internship program which pays $60hr in the Palo Alto area with a $5k sign on bonus. Only a select bunch of the hackers that attended will receive the internship offer, and through winning this hackathon i’m pretty much guaranteed the offer.

With that being said I would’ve never been invited to this event had I not enrolled in this program, so I just wanted to say thanks to Aman and the team for all the value. I applied all the techniques and followed up dozens of times with various recruiters ensuring that I received an invitation to the event and it paid off.

Thanks again to the SWE Accelerator crew.

-side note i’m pretty cracked at hackathons and if you would like to connect and attend a hackathon together feel free to reach out.

post.title: Sharing my Job Search & LinkedIn Automation Setup
post.content:
Hey there!

[@Yvonne Wang](obj://user/1d66bc8d93824f2f8dca9652eb30da53) asked me to share my job search/Linkedin automation and my super simple Job/Referral tracker with you all, I hated doing it. So just tried to remove the friction. Hopefully it helps!

To being with you would need perplexity premium, which is free for a year for anyone with a valid student email. You can use this link [https://pplx.ai/ast1044](https://pplx.ai/ast1044).

Prompt#1 to find job posted in the last 72 hrs for new grads withing 2hrs of the GTA\(Greater Toronto Area\).
`Search for top 3 companies located in the Greater Toronto Area or within a 2-hour driving radius of Toronto \(including Guelph, Kitchener, London, Ottawa\) that are currently hiring junior or new grad software developers. Only include postings from the last 3 days. Return the company name, job title, location, LinkedIn job link, and the official company website link if available.`

Prompt#2 to verify those jobs are valid by checking the company’s website
`For the below companies hiring junior or new grad software developers in the Greater Toronto Area or nearby cities, then for each, check their official careers page to confirm if the role listed on LinkedIn is still posted there. Provide YES/NO, the company job link, and highlight any important differences between LinkedIn and company postings.`

Prompt#3 Find LinkedIn people from that website to contact
`For each verified company with a YES for the job posting on their website and job, search LinkedIn for employees in technical or hiring roles \(Software Engineer, Seneca Graduate,Recruiter, Engineering Manager, Technical Recruiter, HR\) with priority given to those based in Canada or the GTA. Return the names, positions, LinkedIn profile links, and department if available, limited to at least 20 contacts per company/job.`

Prompt#4 Will help you to make a connection message
`For each verified job and company hiring junior software developers in the GTA area, find up to 20 relevant LinkedIn employees \(Software Engineers, Recruiters, Engineering Managers, etc.\).

For each person, generate a personalized LinkedIn connection message under 300 characters using this template:

"Hi \[NAME\], I wanted to connect as I am a recent Software Development grad and would love to work at \[COMPANY\]. I’d love to learn more about you and your experience if you’re available!"

Return the LinkedIn profile link and the full message for each contact, ready for me to copy-paste when sending connection requests.`

Here’s my stupid simple job and referral tracker: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1N0fi5xte2tuhfsDrCNrGEHjtwk7zcgv-7iYy4QITmLc/edit?usp=sharing](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1N0fi5xte2tuhfsDrCNrGEHjtwk7zcgv-7iYy4QITmLc/edit?usp=sharing)

I tried to articulate it, but let me know if you want a voice over video with detailed steps.

This is just an attempt to help me apply for jobs and not procrastinate. Let me know if you have any suggestions to improve it.

post.title: Tesla Offer!
post.content:
I woke up this morning to some wonderful news—I was extended a SWE Internship offer @Tesla with the Factory Software Team!

post.title: Recruiter = Biggest Ally
post.content:
Remember this!!

Recruiters will be your🫶 "Bestie" 🫶throughout the job search process.

Recruiters are evaluated on how quickly they can fill open roles at the company. This means they're just as invested in you succeeding through the interview process as you are! Their goal is to get you into that awesome new job as fast as possible. On top of that timing, providing you with satisfactory candidate experience is a top priority.

Are you leaning on your recruiter and building that rapport with them?

I'm telling you, recruiters should be your secret sauce and you need to keep them on your personal squad.

[ul][li]Come prepared with your perfect ice breaker to kick thing off![li]🤩Fun example was yesterday was Mario Day *3/10* and the candidate found out the recruiter was a total Super Mario fanatic and the candidate was able to kick off the call with a huge laugh and instant connection with the recruiter.[li]Forge that close bond with your recruiter, if recruiters cannot place you in their job, they can push you off to their colleagues that could use your talent![li]Be responsive when they reach out and let them know that you are excited for the role.[li]Most importantly, know recruiter's position.

SO here is my questions for all of you ⁉️

What was a fun, exciting moment where you were able to connect with a recruiter you had interacted with?

What did you experience, learn or appreciate \(or dislike\) about the interaction?

Your insightful stories could really help others navigate the hiring process so who will be brave to kick us off with sharing first?!

post.title: Google Interviews
post.content:
I recently completed two interviews with Google for the Software Engineering Intern position. I performed well in the first interview — the interviewer seemed impressed with my approach and communication. However, the second interview didn’t go as well. I struggled to fully understand the problem, proposed an incorrect approach, and because the interviewer wasn’t very collaborative, I continued with that approach and implemented the code. Unfortunately, my solution didn’t pass the test cases, and we ran out of time. I was also quite nervous during that part.

Now, I’m wondering whether this means I’ll be rejected entirely, or if there’s still a chance that I might be given a third interview, as I’ve heard that some candidates have been asked for a third interview. If anyone has experienced this before, I’d really appreciate hearing whether my case sounds similar or if it’s likely a final rejection.

descriptionText:
Mock interviews are one of the most valuable tools in your preparation. The closer you can simulate a real interview experience before the actual thing, the more confident and composed you'll be when it counts. Here's a breakdown of the mock types available to you.

Coding Mock Interviews (Max 4)

Full live coding interview simulations with expert feedback on your problem-solving approach, communication and coding technique. 

These sessions replicate the pressure of a real technical interview so you can identify gaps and sharpen your skills before the real thing.

Make sure you've worked through the relevant course modules before booking.

Behavioral Mock Interviews (Max 2)

Simulated behavioral interviews with structured feedback based on real-world FAANG-style questions. 

These sessions are designed to help you tell your story clearly, handle curveball questions confidently, and communicate your experience in a way that resonates with interviewers.

Come prepared with your key stories and experiences ready to discuss.

Flex Mock Interviews (Max 2)

Flex mocks are yours to use however you need them most. Use them as an additional behavioral or coding mock, or as focused prep for a specific company or role you're targeting. 

Because they're valid for 6 months you can save them for a moment in your job search when the stakes are highest.

Click here for instructions on how to book a flex mock interview.

descriptionText:
Choose the coach you want to do your mock interview with (listed below)

Click the scheduling link for that coach (listed below)

On the scheduling page, select a time that suits you

Fill out the booking form and schedule the call

Limit: No more than one mock per day

Exception: Multiple bookings in a day require written approval from your coach

If unapproved multiple bookings are found, we will:
Keep the mock that best fits the coach's schedule

Cancel the remaining bookings

How to sign up for Flex Mock Interviews

Complete the pre-submission form before booking anything

In the form, tell us:
What interview or role you are preparing for

What you have already tried or practiced

What you want to get out of the session

At the end of the form, click through to the booking form on Calendly

Fill out the booking form and confirm your session

No-Show & Late Policy

If you RSVP and do not show up, your mock session will be deducted.

If you need to cancel, please notify the host at least 24 hours in advance. Cancellations made less than 24 hours before the session, without a valid reason (e.g., an emergency), will result in a mock session deduction.

If you arrive more than 10 minutes late, you may not be admitted to the session, which will also result in a mock session deduction.

Mock Interview Scheduling Links

Behavioral Mock Interview Link

Book Directly with Yvonne

Book Directly with Jon

Coding Mock Interview Link

Book Directly with Henry

Book Directly with Nikhil

Book Directly with Peter

Book Directly with Uma

Book Directly with Brian

Getting the most out of your mocks

1. Come prepared – Have your questions ready in a notes document before joining.

2. Be specific – Provide relevant details so coaches can give tailored advice.

3. Engage actively – Ask, participate, and take notes.

4. Follow program structure – Watch course modules before asking questions in office hours.

5. Stay consistent – Regular attendance increases success rates significantly.

descriptionText:
Choose the coach you want to do your flex session with

Click the scheduling link for that coach

Select a time that suits you

Fill out the booking form and schedule the session

No-Show / Late Policy

If you RSVP and do not show up, your Flex session will be deducted.

If you need to cancel, please notify the host at least 24 hours in advance. Cancellations made less than 24 hours before the session, without a valid reason (e.g., an emergency), will result in a Flex session deduction.

If you arrive more than 10 minutes late, you may not be admitted to the session, which will also result in a Flex session deduction.

When to use flex sessions

• You missed regular office hours and need urgent help.

• You’re stuck on a specific problem and need one-on-one guidance.

• You want to do a deep dive into a mock interview or a specific technical topic.

Maximizing your flex sessions

Be Prepared: Have specific questions or topics ready to maximize your time. The more detailed you are, the more valuable feedback you’ll get.

Be Respectful of Time: Keep your focus on the most critical issues to make the most of your session.

Follow the Format: Just like in the Community, use the 1-3-1 Format to present your situation clearly:
1 Context Statement: Briefly explain your situation or problem.

3 Options/Approaches: Outline a few ways you’re considering tackling it.

1 Preferred Solution: Mention what you’re leaning toward and why.

Using a Flex Session as a Mock Interview

If you'd like to use a flex session as a mock interview, let your coach know and it will be recorded as a mock ONLY IF your coach is free afterward (the session will run the full 45 minutes).

If your coach has someone after you, you will either need to reschedule or shorten the session to 30 minutes (it will still count as a mock interview).

If you have used all your allocated mock interviews, your flex session cannot be converted to a mock on the spot. Please email us at help@manazir.org about additional mock interviews.

⚠️ Important Reminder: You have a total of 4 Flex Sessions to use throughout the program. Make sure to save them for critical situations and prioritize attending regular Office Hours whenever possible.

descriptionText:
Navigate to the Calendar on Skool

Select an available OH session that fits your schedule

Click the zoom link to register for the session

Submit your question in the registration form at least 20 minutes before the session starts

Click ‘Add to calendar’

A few things to keep in mind:

Submitting your question at registration helps your coach prepare a more useful session for everyone

OH is open to active students only. If your program status is paused, terminated or graduated you will not be able to register

Technical OH is capped at 10 participants — register early to secure your spot. All other OH sessions remain open.

If you join without registering in advance you are welcome to listen but your questions won't be answered in that session

What to expect in OH

Office Hours provide real-time guidance to help you optimise your job search and interview preparation. In 60 minutes, the session will cover:

Open Q&A with our expert coaches

Resume, LinkedIn, application and networking strategy reviews

Behavioral interview preparation

To get the most out of the program we recommend joining at least 2 sessions per week. You may attend an unlimited number of office hours per week but you are required to attend a minimum of 16 OH sessions within the intensive period of the Accelerator program.

How OH sessions are run

The coach for the session reviews pre-submitted questions and will respond to questions that haven’t been answered before.

It's always worth doing a quick search in Skool before submitting your question.

Technical Office Hours

Focused on LeetCode, coding interviews and problem-solving. 

Hosted by experienced engineers from top companies.

Submitting your specific coding question or problem at registration helps your coach make the session more valuable for you.

title: 200+ applications, 3 interviews — what am I missing?
content:
I've been in the accelerator for a while and have been applying the strategies from the videos and homework: applying within 24 hours of a posting going live, tailoring my resume for each role, using a top-1%-reviewed resume and LinkedIn with quantified metrics, and following up with cold outreach for referrals.

Results so far: 200+ applications \(FAANG, non-FAANG, startups, remote, in-person, etc.\) across this cycle and last, using an AI tool called Jobright to target roles that fit my background. Only 3 interview offers at relatively unknown companies, and all 3 came from cold applications rather than referrals — none were top-choice companies. 5 people submitted referrals for me last cycle and none converted to an interview. Cold outreach on LinkedIn/email gets ignored roughly 95% of the time even with a tailored message.

My resume includes a hackathon placement \(6th of 125 teams\) and a related project \(AutiKit\), on top of internship experience.

I'm trying to figure out if this is normal variance for SWE roles, or if there's something structural I'm missing — ATS filtering, resume formatting, outreach approach, timing. I tailor my resume every time to match the keywords for each job post, but it seems like it is not working. Resume attached in the post.

Has anyone hit a similar wall and found what actually moved the needle? Any advice would help. Thanks!

title: The momentum is finally real
content:
Hey everyone,

I wanted to share a quick win and a reminder to keep pushing.

For a long time, the grind was brutal. In my first six months of searching, I only managed to land four total interviews. It gets heavy, and it tests your patience.

Fast forward to today: I’ve had four interviews in the last seven days alone. Companies I don't even remember applying for \(but I did\) are reaching out to me. Recruiters are calling my phone multiple times a day to set up an interview.

I can tell my Resume and LinkedIn page is working.

Seeing all that tracking finally pay off is the most rewarding feeling. If you're in the trenches right now wondering if your applications are going into a black hole, don't stop. It truly comes down to persistence, refining your approach, and refusing to give up.

Rooting for everyone here.

title: AWS Offer |  TC 185k
content:
-1. 14 months summed up in 2 minutes
-2. TLDR Takeaways \(For job seekers you can skip to just this. Takeaways section 2 is the actionable advice.\)

This is just a personal \(opinionated\) reflection of my experience.

1.
I started searching May 2025 14 months ago for a new grad job. My process was not like most at all. The problem was that I am pretty bad at interviewing. Throughout these 14 months, I’ve gone through so many dozens of company interviews, one time I did so bad the guy left the call 20 minutes in \(was scheduled for 90 minutes\). Looking at the facts objectively, it’s of course pretty hardhitting when you fail an interview but I was failing in the dozens. E.g. I had interviews at mainly startups \(because I mainly had startup experience\) in LLD, HLD, agentic system design, behavioral, codebase/DSA, Ai coding. That might seem like a bunch of random topics which is absolutely true, but startups never have a strict formula so I honestly had to topic switch a lot and really attempt multitasking \(its not that much work if you look step-by-step\) . At the time, here I was some guy with a terrible gpa \(primarily last year and whatever I was supposed to learn in theory of comp is still a theory to me\), bad at all interview types, and literally had to learn literally all these interview types independently through random online resources because i wasnt the most high performing student in college.

For added context, 14 months ago I was still in school \(senior year\) and interning at this company Scale ai which continued on for many months. I remember 10 months ago \(while still interning\) I got an email i could interview at scale possible RO! i remember that I was completely grinding \(didnt go to class first 2 weeks of spring semester technically it was still a syllabus week, skipped literally probaly everything including hanging out with friends\) and was probably the most I’ve ever tried for something. I posted on skool to make a prep plan even lol. I remember I was trying so hard. Which is somewhat similar to what anyone else in my position would do if they’ve been trying ~5 apps/day, ~10 connections/day, ~ 1 LC/day, + for months and finally got something pretty nice, sweet chance. I was also working there for some months so felt like I’d do pretty good while preparing. I tried decently hard during this internship \(doing school signup events, weekly pings to my boss, 30+ hrs/week\) so I felt like at that point I got it in the bag. Then, after 2 weeks the day arrived and I was feeling prepped. The call started fantastic he was like “what i didnt know you were an intern seems weird im interviewing you” and he was starting to be even the best interviewer wanting to help out even i remember he wrote a line or two in the coderpad. Then the question appeared… the interview ended just 30 minutes after but I completely failed the interview. I remember i started walking for 4 hours heading northwest with my head in a daze.. knowing that just the next day and months after I would continue to work at a company with no chance of RO and just feeling distraught unfortunately.

title: Passed Google Onsite, but team lost headcount. Next steps?
content:
Hi everyone, I recently completed my Google onsite \(final round\) for an L4 iOS role in NYC. It was really cool, I got to go see the NYC campus. Overall, it's been a great experience, but unfortunately, I got some bittersweet news.

I got an email last week about a status update, and I was feeling good since a call usually means good news. Today I chatted with the recruiter and found out the team I interviewed for lost headcount and closed the role. The good news: I was one of the top candidates \(top 3 for that hiring manager\) and would've advanced to the final stage \(a team-matching fit call with her\) if the role had survived.

So instead of ending there, the recruiter is rerouting me: she'll team-match me with other teams first so a team can champion my packet, then take me to hiring committee. I've let her know I'm open to L3 roles \(not just L4\) and flexible on location. The good news is that she's already reached out to teams about me and has asked me to look for any roles where I match the requirements.

For those who've interviewed at Google or been through something similar — I'd love advice on turning this into an offer. Recruiting mentors, your perspective is very welcome too.

Where I'm at:

[ul][li]Finished L4 iOS onsite ~2 weeks ago, did well enough to be routed to team matching.[li]Feedback is mixed — strong on behavioral + mobile, weaker on one coding round.[li]Haven't gone to Hiring Committee yet. Plan: team-match first so a team champions the packet, then Hiring Committee.[li]iOS at Google is almost all in CA right now. I'm flexible \(NYC top option, Seattle, California, Texas would are the locations I mentioned but also said general USA\).[li]Have a strong employee referral.

I talked to some people in my network who are at Google, they said that team matching can take months but it's not a bad sign. So I will stay proactive and look for opportunities and communicate with my recruiter.

Questions:
[ol:1][li]For anyone who's team-matched, what worked?[li]What's a general timeline for this team-matching stage?[li]How can I leverage my network and/or LinkedIn to open doors?

title: Rewriting My Resume: Do Keyword-First Bullets Work Better?
content:
Hello all, I would really appreciate a guidance as I'm trying to rewrite my resume since I'm not getting much traction with my current version.
I noticed that several peers who landed interviews at MAANG companies used a bullet format similar to this:

• React, Python + AWS: Architected clinician platform from scratch, taking pet sample intake through vet alerts and prescription guidance into one workflow.
• Real-time alerting logic: Built a system that flags unsafe urine sample results on upload, routing cases directly to veterinarians instead of the standard review queue.
• Vector database + AI model: Designed a pipeline that grounds prescriptions in a pet's treatment history, increasing recommendation trust scores by 70%.
• Evaluation harness \(200 prompts\): Built a testing framework that runs on every prompt or model change, catching poor model outputs before they reach clinic operators.
• AWS RDS + S3: Migrated the data layer off Supabase, giving the team full control over clinic data and infrastructure.

My previous resume bullets looked more like this:

• Built a full-stack React and FastAPI triage workspace that reduced manual review overhead by 40% across 200 clinic users, enabling real-time adoption of AI-assisted case triage.
• Designed the user onboarding flow for AI-assisted prescription review, instrumenting activation metrics and iterating on UX feedback to drive engagement.
• Owned end-to-end feature delivery for a pgvector-backed RAG pipeline that surfaces clinical context from patient history.

I'm curious which style recruiters and hiring managers find easier to scan.

My intuition is that leading with the key technology or system area \(followed by a colon\) makes it easier to quickly understand both the stack and the impact, especially during a fast resume review.

Has anyone experimented with this format or seen better results using it and should I do it?

Thank you for you time and help!

title: Entrepreneur Route and Wins
content:
It's been one year since I joined Aman Manazir's Software Engineering Accelerator, and I just wanted to say thank you. Joining this community completely changed the trajectory of my career.

Before joining, I had never been to a hackathon. Because of the Accelerator, I started attending them, and at a Snowflake startup competition I met someone who would later become my cofounder.

Together we:
[ul][li]Won 2nd place out of 40 teams.[li]Presented our startup to investors through Snowflake.[li]Got accepted into Confluent's accelerator program.

Although the startup eventually came to an end, the experience opened doors I never thought I'd have and taught me more than I could have imagined.

The community also encouraged me to attend SHPE, where I traveled to Philadelphia by myself without knowing anyone. Once I got there, I ended up meeting several people even some from the Accelerator, made some great connections, and even landed an interview with Apple after previously struggling to get interviews.

Looking back, I realize this is probably the lowest-risk point in my life. I don't have major financial obligations or people depending on me yet, so if I'm ever going to bet on myself and build something, now is the time. Even if I fail, I'll gain experience and be able to recover.

None of this would have happened if I hadn't joined this community. Every opportunity seemed to lead to another one, and it all started with simply deciding to get involved.

So thank you, Aman, and thank you to everyone in this community. I genuinely don't think I'd be on this path without you.

If you'd like to follow my journey, I'm now building a music-learning app called Pianiso. I'm just getting started this month, but I'd love to have you along for the ride.

title: 🙌 Shoutout to Joshua!
content:
Joshua submitted a bug report and a design suggestion for the Ship Log.

What Joshua caught: Logging proof of work during a grace period was dropping entries into the wrong cycle. He didn’t leave the notes column blank or just write ‘better UI’, he suggested a fix.

What we built: To log work from a previous cycle, simply select that cycle from the cycle picker before submitting \(see attached image\). If submission falls within the grace period, it'll submit as usual. If it falls outside of the grace period, it will also be accepted but marked as a 'late submission'.

Example:
A cycle ends June 14.
On June 17 you remember a LeetCode problem you still have to submit.

title: Second SWE offer post layoff — Actifai
content:
Update: a second offer, and it came the exact same way the first one did.

Two weeks ago I posted about my first SWE offer post-layoff. I now have a second offer, Actifai, an AI startup in DC. So I'm somewhere I genuinely didn't think I'd be 9 months ago: choosing between two offers.

[ul][li]Of my 4 other pipelines, Esri and GDMS passed, I'm stepping back from ECS Federal, and Actifai converted to an offer.[li]It came through a referral: a friend from Walmart connected me to someone on the inside who flagged the opening. Warm intro -> conversations -> offer

Two things I learned this round:

[ol:1][li]The referral thesis held. Again. Both of my offers came through warm intros, not the 1500+ cold apps. Peraton via an employee referral, Actifai via a friend of a friend. [@Aman Manazir](obj://user/83840ae6dab145bb851045e0e0ca6c63) 's "one warm intro > 50 cold applications" is NOT a slogan, it's literally what just happened to me, twice.[li]One offer is leverage for all the others. Having Peraton in hand changed every converstion that followed. Being transparent about my timeline turned a "maybe someday" pipeline into a fast, real offer. A bird in hand isn't just a floor, it ACCELERATES everyone else.

I have to make the call this week, but wanted to share while it's fresh. To everyone grinding in the deep end, it compounds. Keep going!!! I joined only 3 months ago!

Huge thanks again to [@Aman Manazir](obj://user/83840ae6dab145bb851045e0e0ca6c63) , [@Jon Gourdet](obj://user/2e79acf24f0843b795cddaa0777036ca) , [@Yvonne Wang](obj://user/1d66bc8d93824f2f8dca9652eb30da53) , [@Peter Wu](obj://user/ff6ebe42c8884a31b18218757d1fcdda) , [@Nikhil Hegde](obj://user/5f7f9e011863414c96fc6141fb0cf23a) !

title: Am I asking for referrals too early? (Tiered Referral Strategy)
content:
Context: Got an Amazon referral, but a "lower-tier" one. There are two tiers apparently to Amazon referrals: "network referrals" and "personal referrals" \(higher tier\). I have two more calls scheduled with other Amazon SWE's.

Question: Since I am asking for referrals in Summer 2027, should I just not ask for a referral on the initial coffee chat, since that'd basically guarantee I'd get the "lower-tier" one?

Instead, I am thinking of doing \(in order\):

[ol:1][li]Initial coffee chat, show genuine curiosity/interest. Find out what team they're working on.[li]Send them a follow up via email/text showing curiosity about a new feature their team released since we last spoke, or some sort of conversation to simulate a continued, non-transactional relationship[li]Schedule another chat closer to the job posting, and ask for the referral then \(hopefully a "higher tier" one\)

In the context of cold leads, do you think this would potentially be a good strategy?

Potential options of mine:
[ol:1][li]Continue to go for the referral within the first 15 min, or[li]Go with the longer approach that I mentioned above, or[li]Play it by ear by how good the initial coffee chat is

Leaning towards #3, but I'm not sure if my "longer approach" is too "fake"/unlikely to help.

Would love to hear from the networking coaches and other students, maybe someone has experience with this!

title: Case Study: Recruiter Referral Rejection
content:
Before I started the Accelerator Program, I had been getting LinkedIn emails from Recruiters for Senior Engineer roles which felt odd because I did a career transition and feel more like a Junior/Mid-level. So I ignored them!

Right before I’m ready to submit my resume for review here, a Recruiter reaches out to me about another Senior position. This time, I engage and tell them I might not be the best fit but to keep me in mind. They then say the company they are working with also has a Junior/Mid-Level role and they’d love to hop on a call. We chatted and they decided to refer me!

I gave them my old resume, waited a week, and the company still turned me down due to lack of experience. After they let me know, I told them I’m happy to still work with them and that I have an updated resume they can work with.

So lessons learned:

Always keep the door open!
Send your most updated info!
Connections are imperative!

title: First SWE offer post-layoff -- Peraton Associate
content:
After 9 months of grinding post-layoff, I got my first written SWE offer this week: Software Engineering Associate at Peraton. Sharing the path + a few things that actually moved the needle, for anyone else in the deep end right now.

The story so far:

[ul][li]VT CS '24 -> Walmart Global Tech intern '24 -> Walmart FT mobile engineer Feb-Aug '25 -> laid off[li]Built CarryRank solo for 9 months \(Python/FastAPI/Postgres/Next.js multi-service ranking platform for bowling\)[li]Currently active in 4 other pipelines: Esri, GDMS, Actifai startup, ECS Federal

Two things actually worked:

Internal referrals beat my 1500+ total applications. Peraton came through an internal-employee referral. Referral -> interview in 7 days. Interview -> offer in 6 days. The cold applications I sent for 9 months prior? Mostly silence. [@Aman Manazir](obj://user/83840ae6dab145bb851045e0e0ca6c63) is correct: one warm intro is worth ~50 cold applications.

Project-shaped > resume-shaped.
I took the advice of making a project with a paywall with [@Jon Gourdet](obj://user/2e79acf24f0843b795cddaa0777036ca) 's advice of shifting as an "experience" even if it's a project. The game is the game. Most recruiters looked at my layoff as a risk with nothing present, with Claude Code, you can build pretty much anything.

title: How to create a great Github profile
content:
I've just began a job as an MLE, for the interview process, I failed the initial OA \(0/600\) and I was still moved on to the next round \(to be fair I had most of the code done, I just ran out of time formatting output\).

In the first interview, the hiring manager told me one of the reasons he felt strong about me was my active Github.

Almost every job posting asks you to link a github, and theres some easy steps you can take to ensure yours stands out:

[ol:1][li]Add a profile picture \(anything as long as its not default\) and basic information: location, name, linkedin.[li]Get the basic achievement badges, most can be completed with a second account [within 5 minutes](https://githubachievements.com/).[li]Get some projects you're proud of and pin them, then share on reddit or hackernews \(or here!\) to get some stars, or if you're[ in a hurry...](https://www.reddit.com/r/opensource/comments/10gesz4/fake_github_stars/)[li]For your contribution graph, theres nothing much to do except try to add a little something to a project every day, and it builds up over time. Again, if desperate, there are [ways around this...](https://github.com/artiebits/fake-git-history)

Everything on this list can be completed within an hour and will guarantee that you stand out from other candidates \(see images below and imagine yourself as a recuiter looking at either profile\)

title: Job Boards
content: We went over this in my office hours: Software Engineering roles, the best approach is using a mix of general job boards, startup platforms, and direct company career pages. [LinkedIn Jobs](https://www.linkedin.com/jobs/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) is one of the strongest overall for recruiter visibility and networking, while [Indeed](https://www.indeed.com/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) is useful for application volume. For startups and fast-growing tech companies, [Wellfound](https://wellfound.com/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) and [Otta](https://otta.com/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) are excellent because they focus heavily on modern tech roles and provide good company transparency. If you want remote SWE opportunities, [Remote OK](https://remoteok.com/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) and [We Work Remotely](https://weworkremotely.com/?utm_source=chatgpt.com). Like I mentioned also get familiar with the Career Pages of the companies you want to work for.

title: SoFi offer!
content:
I got my second offer this month and wanted to shared with everybody how I got there! I joined the program on February 17th, had 2 unpaid internships and Community college in a resume with 3.2 GPA. I graduate in December 2026 and my goal was to land summer internship in a range 25-40$/hr.
Until the end of the march I had only 3 interviews, that mostly end at screening stage. After that I thought that I am doing something wrong, build an AI related project \(RAG Document Q&A\) + updated my resume to make it more metrics heavy, and started tracking and rating each position I am applying to. I would give a claude my resume and all the disqualifiers and if the position is higher then 6 I would apply and claude would add it to excel file. The rating would be based on tech stack, location, salary, company and etc.
During an April I applied around 150 times with 5 total interview from which I got 2 offers and 4 final rounds! First offer: Company name is SitusAMC it’s 25$/hr very easy interview process and remote. Second offer \(one that I picked\): Company name is SoFi it’s 55$/hr + 5k relocation stipend to SF. The interview process had 2 technical Leetcode style interviews \(the only company that did Leetcode style interview with me\) and 2 behaviour interviews with engineering managers from different teams.
Want to say huge thanks to all the coaches! Without mock interviews I wouldn’t be able to get through this process! Each interview make it a little bit easier, but I feel like you will never be fully ready, so the only option it’s just to practice as much as possible and hope for the best!
I attached my resume and excel file, so everyone could check them out and hope it would be helpful to at least somebody!

title: Considered for a Senior Role as a Mid-Level Engineer
content:
I recently got considered for a Senior Machine Learning Engineer position that I applied to almost by chance.

My resume is mainly positioned for mid-level ML roles, and the job requirements actually match my background and years of experience.

However, after reviewing the responsibilities more carefully, the role seems broader than what I have fully owned before. It involves leading deployment and delivery of ML models across multiple architectures, designing low-latency inference systems.

I now have a recruiter screen call tomorrow, and I would really appreciate advice from you guys and any Engineers who have been in a similar situation.

My main question is:
How should I position myself honestly and confidently when the requirements match my resume, but some of the responsibilities are slightly above my current hands-on ownership level?

The three options I am considering:
[ol:1][li]Be transparent with the recruiter and say I meet the core requirements, but I see the role as a stretch opportunity where I can grow into the broader system ownership responsibilities.[li]Ask directly about the expected level, team support, ramp-up period, and whether the role is more execution-focused or senior ownership-focused.[li]Continue with the process, prepare deeply around ML inference systems, low-latency deployment, system design, then let the interview process determine the fit.

Would love to hear your advice on how to handle this professionally without underselling myself or overclaiming experience.

title: Accepted QT offers at SIG and Akuna
content:
Hey everyone, I'm a bit late to posting this but I'm excited to share that I'll be at SIG this summer as a quantitative trading intern!

I already did the Akuna "internship" \(it was a one week micro-internship\) in January though lol.

The journey was tough but also really fun and rewarding. I'm not the biggest fan of coding so prepping probability/math/logic problems was really refreshing, especially after all the leetcode I was slugging through before.

Big thanks to [@Aman Manazir](obj://user/83840ae6dab145bb851045e0e0ca6c63) for the direction throughout. The podcast with your brother talking about QT was really interesting to watch and was great info throughout.

For anyone curious about quant prep specifically, the stuff that moved the needle for me outside of LeetCode was Zetamac for mental math, A Practical Guide to Quantitative Finance Interviews \(the green book\) for a basic understanding of what you might see in interviews, and [https://www.quantable.io/](https://www.quantable.io/) or [https://www.quantguide.io/questions](https://www.quantguide.io/questions) for more rigorous "leetcode-styled" practice.

Thank you to everyone in this community for the help and guidance!

title: Morgan Stanley Recruiter withdraws offer
content:
I applied Morgan Stanley early December and went through the following process:
[ul][li]Round 1 in December[li]Round 2 and round 3 in February with 2 different teams.[li]3 weeks later I got a rejection email[li]Another 3 weeks later got a "moving forward" \(Their pick 1 fell through and I was second\)

I met the team again we talked and I thought it was a great fit, they did too. Recruiter tells me there's a ton of admin and I'd get an offer soon.

A week later she called me saying congrats I got the offer. We negotiated and agreed on compensation. She said I would get official offer letter in a week.

A week later she calls me saying there was an internal restructure/budget cuts and they no longer could hire me. She said the teams liked me and were excited to onboard me but it was out of their control. She also said she was sorry and she would try to see internally if other teams/department needed someone.

I know there are many roles open and that continue to open and I'm sure they would much rather interview or give priority to someone who already passed the technical bar instead of starting from scratch with someone who might not pass round 1.

My questions are:
How can I make the best of this situation?
What should I ask the recruiter, hiring manager or the engineers who interviewed me?
How can I maximize my chances of receiving an offer again \(even if it's long term like 60 or 90 days\)?

Thank you :\)

title: Different approach to securing an interview
content:
Hi everyone,
I managed to get an interview with a really fast growing decently sized start up recently.

It started when I sent to a hackathon, it was a two day event. At the end of the first day, I decided to pivot from creating content from the hackathon to creating an MVP software for one of the CEOs that were speaking there.

Come the next day, the MVP was barely ready but still it was functional enough that the CEO asked me to send him my resume alongside the repo of the project.That translated over to a meeting with the VP of engineering for that company.

At the meeting the VP mentioned that this was a very impressive approach and that I was doing things right.

He said that while they don’t take full time new grad employees. He will try to set me up for an interview for an internship/ contractual position which will lead to a full time position provided that everything is right.

I’m hoping that landing a contract will later on lead to a full time position.

It’s a big win in my eyes so I just wanted to post in case anyone wanted to take a similar approach.

title: 3 Internship Offers
content:
Hello everyone,

I'm beyond happy to share that I received 3 internship offers this recruiting season.

When I finished my freshman year in May 2025, I set a goal for myself - get an internship before the end of sophomore year. For a year, I worked toward it. I joined the Software Accelerator in January, and four months later, I have three offers in hand.

The one thing everyone in my life told me when I set that goal? "It's hard for a sophomore to get an internship — wait until junior year." This program broke that belief entirely. A few months ago, I wasn't even getting replies to my applications. Today, I have three offers. It still feels surreal.

It started with one LinkedIn message to Aman. He asked me to join the program - and that single moment changed the trajectory completely

To the coaches - your guidance is a goldmine. To everyone in this program - If you follow the guidance, you will find your way for sure! title: Passed Interview with Hiring Manager
content:

On to the technical round!

title: Interview!
content:
Just wrapped up an interview at DTCC, I was going into it feeling nervous, not knowing what to expect. It was mostly technical, with some behavioral questions too.

I expected it to be very backend heavy, despite being a full-stack role. I decided to be honest with the interviewer and shared that while I've done backend work, my focus is definitely more on the frontend.

It went surprisingly well \(I think\)! We discussed my experience, talked through some high-level concepts \(I needed to ask some clarifying questions, but I think my answers were mostly received well\). Then they asked me some behavioral questions. Thankfully, I had recently done a mock with Yvonne and her feedback was very useful here - thanks Yvonne!

Not sure if I'll advance, but I am feeling good about the interview and I had a chance to brush up on some important contexts.

Some things that I think helped me on this interview.

[ol:1][li]When I was in a corporate setting: I asked A LOT of questions. Even if I didn't build something, I understood it and how it connected to the overall project.[li]I build a lot of projects outside of work. Even though I've leaned heavily into vibe coding - this has helped me understand system design on a very practical level.[li]I was honest. I didn't fake my way through the interview and I think the interviewer appreciated that and helped to guide me on the questions that I lacked some context on.[li]I didn't cram, I focused on what I knew and went into the interview with good sleep, a morning run, and a nice breakfast. I think it helped me stay composed and focused.

Keep grinding team!

title: 8 Months in the Search – From FAANG Interviews to a Sudden Standstill
content:
I’m reaching out because I’ve hit a bit of a wall. I’ve been a part of this community for 8 months now, and while I’ve stayed consistent, the recent silence is starting to get to me.

The Current Rut: Since February, everything has died down significantly. Despite maintaining my routine, the "funnel" has dried up. Here is what my daily grind looks like:

[ul][li]Applications: Minimum of 5 tailored applications per day.[li]Technical Prep: Consistent LeetCode \(Blind 75/NeetCode 150\) and system design review.[li]Soft Skills: Regular mock interviews to keep my communication sharp.

The Reality Check: I went from high-stakes interviews at major tech giants to hardly getting a screening call in the last few weeks. It feels like I’m doing the work, but the market or my strategy isn't clicking like it was a few months ago.

I’d love to hear from anyone who has been in this 6–9 month "dead zone": How did you pivot your strategy when your initial leads dried up?

Appreciate any insights or reality checks you all can offer. Still grinding, just looking for the light at the end of the tunnel.

title: FT SWE Interview Prep Advice
content:
I’ve recently gone through a few Full-Time New Grad/Entry-Level SWE interviews recently, and I’m noticing a clear difference compared to internship interviews. These FT interviews tend to go much deeper technically. Things like language-specific questions, Unix/Linux fundamentals, data structures like Tries, system design, and more. To make things worse, most companies don't tell you specifics on what to expect, so it makes tailoring your prep even harder. As a result, I have not been successful in landing a Full-Time offer yet.

Because of that, I feel the current program is geared more toward internship prep. Now that I’m applying for Full-Time SWE roles, I’d really appreciate guidance or resources tailored for this level of technical depth. Full-Time interviews often expect you to “know everything about everything,” which makes it tough to build a focused study plan. The Pareto set and LeetCode alone are not going to be sufficient enough any more.

Would [@Aman Manazir](obj://user/83840ae6dab145bb851045e0e0ca6c63) or any of the technical coaches be able to help point me in the right direction or provide support for a complete comprehensive Full-Time SWE interview prep guide? I feel a lot of students would benefit from this. Thanks!

title: Should I be actively applying to FAANG level internships while on Step 2 of the Stairway Framework?
content:
Hi everyone, hope you're all doing well!

I joined the Software Engineering Accelerator Program on March 23rd, completed the orientation module, and am currently 56% through the Foundations module. After going through the Stairway Framework video and completing the quiz, I was placed on Step 2, which left me uncertain about how to structure my focus going forward.

Question:
Should I be actively applying to FAANG level internships right now at Step 2, or should I wait until I've progressed further in the program?

3 potential solutions:
1. Start applying to FAANG internships now, even at Step 2 and use the application process itself as a learning experience and treat early rejections as low-stakes practice.
2. Hold off on FAANG applications until I've moved up a step, so my technical skills are stronger before I face interviews.
3. Apply selectively and target a few FAANG companies with later recruiting timelines \(e.g., Meta, Google\) while continuing to build skills, rather than doing a full application push.

1 recommendation \(the solution that I'm leaning towards\):
I'd lean toward Option 3 which means applying selectively to companies with longer runways while continuing to progress through the program.

Thank you for all of your insights.

title: Getting Interviews
content:
Over the last month, I applied around 100 times, had around 10 referrals, and also contacted recruiters twice. I got 4 screenings out of all of this:
[ol:1][li]0 came from companies where I applied with a referral, probably because most of them were big companies like Walmart or TikTok.[li]I contacted recruiters twice, and both times I got screenings and interviews with hiring managers, which I unfortunately failed, but getting them was already progress for me.

Even though the sample size is small, I found that contacting recruiters has the highest ROI, at least for me, so I wanted to post about it here and explain how to do it:
[ol:1][li]Do not contact recruiters on LinkedIn — you will probably get ghosted. The best thing to do is try to find an email. You can ask people who already got an internship at your target company, or use a site like RocketReach. I think you can check around 5 people for free, but I am not sure since I only recently found out about it.[li]Do not text just any recruiter from the company. Ideally, you need to find a recruiter from the city you are applying to, and if it is for an internship, it should be a university recruiter. Sometimes the position has a hiring manager listed on LinkedIn — that is the best.[li]I suggest doing this only for positions that look like a strong fit for you and align most with your skill set. At least that is what I did, because in my opinion, all it does is increase the chance of your resume being seen.

For those who interested: I am applying to mid size companies for SWE Summer Internships.

Hope this information was helpfull, and I would love to hear mentors' opinions on it!

title: I created a Claude Code skill to get LinkedIn Connections
content:
Hey everyone, it's been a while since I've been here.

Once I got a job as a software engineer and I kind of just stopped looking at Skool. Sorry about that.

However, I've been back on the hunt and I've been trying to grow my LinkedIn connections.

I actually created a Claude Code workflow that navigates LinkedIn and automatically sends connection requests \(with notes\) to people at your school.

I've been using it for about two weeks and I've gained about a hundred connections in that time. Almost all of those connections are actively working software engineers.

It's extremely useful, obviously slower than humans, but it works in the background and it's easy to start. So let me know if this is something you guys would be interested in me posting.

The [skill.md](http://skill.md) file is attached.

****** PLEASE READ BEFORE USING ********

LinkedIn does not like bots.
Don't do more than 50 connections per day.
There are some things in this skill that purposely force synchronous actions DO NOT REMOVE THEM.
The skill prevents having +2 tabs going at a single time.
This is done on purpose. It prevents lag and prevents you getting banned.
If you do have multiple agents working in parallel you could very easily get banned.

**** You've been warned. Use it at your own risk ****

I've been using it for 2 weeks now with no issues \(30 connections / day\).
If I do have an issue I will let you know.

Change this skill to fit your needs and setup.

My skill uses Obsidian CLI + Skill and Playwright CLI + Skill.

I would recommend using these tools but it's up to you.

title: Following Up 10 times ACTUALLY works!
content: Hi friends, I just wanted to share a specific experience I've had recently with Aman's strategy of consistently following up with people. This ACTUALLY works, and I cannot stress how important it is to stay consistent. I had messaged this person 6 times before she finally responded! I would usually message her every 2-3 days because I wanted a referral for the company she works at. Although she was clearly annoyed that I "spammed" her, it didn't matter because I was able to get her to respond and move forward with my request. Aside from this, I have already scheduled 10+ meetings and gotten 5+ referrals within just 1 week. I'd recommend creating a google spreadsheet to track all the people you need to follow up on and send those follow ups daily. The key takeaway here is to stay consistent and to not worry about "bothering" someone because you're literally 1 referral/conversation away from landing that first interview. Hope this helps and have a great week!

title: Tailoring Resume to Jobs
content:
I’ve been tailoring my resume for every SWE internship I apply to. I paste the job description and attach my resume into ChatGPT/Claude, adjust my bullets to reflect the posting, and try to align with required skills. Despite this, I’ve received over 10 rejections without interviews despite tailoring each time.

On Jobright and LinkedIn, I often see “strong fit” or 90% match scores — but that hasn’t translated into interviews.

I’d appreciate advice on three things:

1\) How deeply should I tailor? Should I explicitly mirror every technical keyword and soft skill from the posting \(e.g., collaboration, communication, cross-functional, AI, machine learning\), or focus mainly on hard skills \(like Python, SQL, C++, etc.\) and quantified impact? How do you balance keyword alignment with maintaining credibility and originality?

2\) How much do referrals actually move the needle? If you had to rank importance, how would you compare:

[ul][li]Very strong resume, no referral[li]Strong resume + strong internal referral[li]Moderate resume + recruiter connection[li]Moderate resume + strong internal referral

\(Assume the moderate resume still meets all baseline qualifications.\)

3\) Looking at my base resume, what structural weaknesses might explain early rejections? Is it positioning? Lack of impact metrics? School? Tech stack signaling? Something else?
I’m trying to debug this systematically rather than just send more applications.

Context: I’m a junior CS student at Oregon State \(3.9 GPA\), with prior internship experience at Abby Care and Qualcomm Institute \(resume attached for reference\), targeting SWE internships. No sponsorship needed.

title: How should I deal with the education section on my resume?
content:
Hello everyone! After advancing through the immigration pipeline, I think I can start applying again to summer internships. However, I have a slight issue with my education section that I'm not sure how to deal with. My freshman year, I was at Boston University but had to drop out due to immigration/financial reasons, and ended up enrolling at my local community college. I am attending there right now and in the process of transferring for Fall 2026.

I am not sure how I should deal with this since many application forms require you to be enrolled in a Bachelor's and expect a graduation date further than this spring \(which I will have just not at the moment\).

I could leave only Boston University up in the education section, and clarify my exact situation once/if I reach a recruiter in the process. But maybe that could be interpreted as misleading since I'm not enrolled there anymore \(it's not a leave of absence\). I did this when I was in the process for Google, and they didn't seem to mind, just asked me a few clarifying questions:

"Please confirm the degree you are currently pursuing and the anticipated graduation date."
"I was pursuing a Bachelor’s degree in Mathematics and Computer Science from which I had to withdraw due to financial reasons. I am currently pursuing an Associate of Arts in Mathematics at Miami Dade College, and planning to graduate in Spring 2026."

"Please confirm the degree you will be pursuing in the Fall of 2026 and the anticipated graduation date."

title: My Cold Referral Tips + Experience (Aman asked me to post this)
content:
💎 DEMO VIDEO : [https://drive.google.com/file/d/1GUXpYUSfHZqv_BwstKK3vr6XMhRyFgt3/view?usp=sharing](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1GUXpYUSfHZqv_BwstKK3vr6XMhRyFgt3/view?usp=sharing)

I started with literally nothing — no connections, no strategy, no idea what I was doing.
Now I’m getting referrals, setting up real conversations, and even getting treated to dinner by people I met on LinkedIn. Wild.

Here’s what I’ve learned so far 👇My LinkedIn:
[https://www.linkedin.com/in/joeyzhangdev/](https://www.linkedin.com/in/joeyzhangdev/)

✍️ Be creative with your connection notes
Keep it warm and human. Imagine getting 50 messages with the same “Hi, I’d love to connect” line. Snoozefest.

When I reach out to someone my age, I write how I text.
[ul][li]Just got a US Bank referral with:“Going from selling boba to SWE is crazy…”[li]Asked a recent grad for a chat using:“Maybe you can make me feel a little less cooked.”
For locals, I ask about their favorite restaurant — just foodie-to-foodie talk. That led to two IRL dinners \(they treated me 💀\).

For bootcamp grads:
“Hi X, I’m a CS + Math student and just wanted to say your journey from \(bootcamp\) into a full-time SWE role at Morgan Stanley is seriously impressive. Breaking into tech from a bootcamp takes real grit — I’d love to connect and hear more about your path!”
Nontraditional paths deserve respect. Example:
“Hi X, I really admired your journey from CPA to full-stack engineer. I really liked the X Project! I’d love to connect and hear more about what helped you along the way.”

⏰ Send messages at the right times
Still testing this, but here’s what’s been working:
[ul][li]Tuesday–Friday mornings or late afternoons \(4–6pm\)[li]Sundays aren’t bad either.[li]Mondays = dead zone. Everyone’s catching up on emails.[li]2am? Only reply you’ll get is from someone on call and suffering.[li]
📊 Use a tracking system
Simple Google Sheet. Must-have. Here’s what I track:
[ul][li]Request Sent Date[li]Connection Date[li]Last & Next Follow-Up[li]Notes, Call Scheduled?[li]Days Remaining \(use formulas\)

title: Resume Tip
content:
When writing out the bullets for your job responsibilities, please remind yourself that majority of recruiters haven't personally held the positions they're recruiting for-- yes that is correct, if you are a software engineer - it is almost always that the recruiter reading your resume has never been in a similar role themselves. Their grasp of the role requirements comes primarily from what hiring managers communicate during the initial intake conversation \(where they discuss the position, target candidate characteristics, hiring timeline, and other key details\)

What does this mean?

Make is effortless for a recruiter without that technical hands on knowledge can easily know what is your role and also how your experiences can translate to value/asset to the business they are supporting.

So please technical keywords for the ATS and recruiter searches + clear explanations for human understanding!! 🚀

title: HackerRank Challenges
content:
Hi everyone,

I wanted to ask for some advice about the HackerRank challenges that companies use as an initial step in their interview process.

I have taken several of these assessments, and I am usually able to solve the first one or two questions. However, the later questions, which are often labeled as medium difficulty, feel extremely challenging. They tend to require techniques or problem solving patterns that I have not encountered before. Even when I come up with a solution, it often fails some of the hidden test cases. I end up spending a lot of time trying to optimize or debug edge cases, and I still do not pass all the tests, which means I do not move on to the next round.

I am trying to better understand what companies are actually evaluating through these assessments. Are they mainly looking for complete correctness across all edge cases, time and space complexity, coding style, or something else? How much does a partially correct solution count compared to one that passes every test case? I am also curious about what recruiters or hiring managers can actually see on their end.

If anyone has insight into how these challenges are evaluated or strategies for approaching the harder problems more effectively, I would really appreciate your advice.

title: Startup role + interview
content:
I recently met the founder of a startup at an in-person event and followed up afterward. Their ops person reached out with a Calendly link \(leads to an interview\) and a Notion/Google-form–style application.

The form asks for basic information, but it also asks what type of role I’d be most interested in. The options include product manager, product design, forward deployed engineer, AI agents engineer, full-stack developer, etc. These feel like roles designed for more senior hires rather than undergraduate interns. I’m genuinely excited by many of these roles, especially because I’m at a stage where I’m interested in both product and technical work, and I’m still exploring what I enjoy most.

Where I’m unsure how to proceed is this:

When I select certain roles \(for example, forward deployed engineer or AI agents engineer\), the form asks me to rate my experience and confidence with specific technical areas such as REST APIs, PostgreSQL, Neo4j, and multi-agent architectures.

I have little exposure to parts of this stack, but I wouldn’t describe myself as highly confident across all of it yet. At the same time, these are exactly the kinds of systems I’m excited to learn and grow into.

So my questions are:
• Should I select a role I’m genuinely interested in and motivated to grow into, even if I don’t yet meet all the technical expectations listed?
• Or should I only select roles where I already have strong, concrete past experience with the required technologies?
• Alternatively, would it be better to choose the “Other / Unlisted” option and define a role for myself?

If I do go with the “Other” option, what kind of role should I frame for myself if my ideal position blends product thinking, customer context, and hands-on technical building, without misrepresenting my current skill level?

I’d love guidance on how to approach this strategically—being honest about where I am today while not underselling my curiosity, learning speed, or potential impact.

title: Bloomberg SWE Interview
content:
Recently, I actually acquired an interview for a Software Engineering role in Princeton, NJ after being referred by a classmate who works out of the NYC office. I didn’t end up moving forward in the process, and I wanted to share a few reflections—both as encouragement and as lessons learned for others currently interviewing.

One thing I think I could’ve done better was how I talked about my projects. In mock interviews, I’ve been coached to avoid long-winded answers, so this time I intentionally tried to be concise. Looking back, I may have overcorrected and ended up being too vague instead of clearly highlighting the depth and impact of my work.

The technical portion involved a histogram-style problem: given two one-dimensional arrays—one containing data points and another defining bucket limits—determine how many values fall into each bucket. I approached it by sorting both arrays and using a HashMap to track counts. The interview itself was very collaborative, and we worked through the logic together.

At one point, I made a small implementation mistake when incrementing a value in the HashMap by attempting to rely on map.get\(...\) + 1 without properly overwriting the key-value pair. The interviewer lightly corrected me without giving the full answer, and I reasoned through it out loud, suggesting that I should use map.put\(...\) to overwrite the existing value with the incremented one. With that nudge, I corrected myself, and the interviewer confirmed the approach.

The entire problem took about 50 minutes to work through \(he only had one problem scheduled\). The interviewer said he was satisfied with the solution, which is part of why I’m honestly a bit puzzled about not being moved forward in the process. The interviewer seemed to like me and seemed to be quite pleased with my solution. I didn’t even need a hint or even ask for a hint for the solution.

That experience reminded me that interviews aren’t evaluated on correctness alone. Clarity, speed, communication, and even comparison against other strong candidates can all factor in—sometimes in ways we don’t get visibility into.

title: Decision Scientists Interview Help!
content:
I have an upcoming interview for a Decision Scientist role.

Based on what the team shared and what I’ve seen on Glassdoor, the interview may include logic-based questions \(for example, puzzles like the 9-digit lock\) along with time series–style reasoning and project discussions.

I’m very comfortable with project-based and scenario-driven questions walking through past work, explaining assumptions, trade-offs, and business impact. Where I find it more challenging is logic-heavy puzzles that are very abstract and time-pressured, since they tend to test focus and pattern recognition more than real-world decision-making.

Here’s how I’m currently approaching preparation:
[ol:1][li]Practicing structured thinking out loud for logic problems, even when I don’t reach the final answer quickly.[li]Revising time series fundamentals with an emphasis on interpretation and business implications rather than formulas.[li]Mapping my past projects to clear decision frameworks so I can explain why certain choices were made, not just what was done.

I’d really appreciate any advice on how to better prepare for logic-based questions in Decision Scientist or analytics interviews, especially ways to stay calm and structured under time constraints.
