title: Build-based interview challenge from a Canadian AI startup — need advice
content:
Looking for advice on a non-traditional interview challenge I just received.
I was applying to Canadian startups and came across Superbar \([superbar.ai](http://superbar.ai)\). I directly messaged the founder with a short pitch about my background. Within ~20 minutes, I got a response — instead of a standard interview, they asked me to build something using AI.
Challenge details:
[ul][li]Build anything using AI[li]No traditional development required — stitching third-party tools is fine[li]Focus on AI workflows / automation, not UI[li]Record a 2–5 min Loom explaining what I built and how & why[li]Emphasis on how things are connected \(tools, logic, decisions\), not a full product demo[li]Simple workflows are preferred \(e.g., “When X happens in tool Y, use AI to do Z and output to tool W”\)[li]If sharing an existing project, the guidance is to focus specifically on the AI components and decision-making
My dilemma:
[ul][li]Should I build something completely new for this?[li]Or reuse an existing AI project and reframe it tightly around AI workflows and system design?
Context on projects I could reference if I go the “existing work” route \(AI-focused only\):
[ul][li]macOS AI Chatbot \(Performance Research Project\)[li]AI Closet \(ML Web App\)[li]Current AI Startup Experience \(Tranquility Inc.\)
Idea I’m currently leaning toward instead:Build a small, fresh AI workflow specifically for this challenge:
[ul][li]New LinkedIn message → AI analyzes intent & conversation stage[li]AI selects the best reply from my pre-written scripts[li]Conversation state is tracked over time[li]If a referral is detected \(e.g., “happy to refer”, “send your resume”\), it logs the interaction into a Google Sheet as a lightweight CRM[li]Human-in-the-loop throughout \(AI suggests, I approve\)

Would love feedback from anyone who’s gone through build-based interviews or early-stage startup hiring — specifically whether building something new like this is the better signal vs. reframing prior AI work.

title: Should you tell an interviewer that you've seen the leetcode question before?
content:
Question as title.

Pros of telling the interviewer:
[ul][li]Shows honesty[li]Interviewer might found out anyways[li]There are usually multiple coding rounds to try and minimize this anyways

Cons of telling the interviewer
[ul][li]With the competition these days, this is a golden opportunity[li]If they ask you to still solve the problem and you can't, that's a big OOF

I would personally side with not telling the interviewer and focus on not the answer, but the problem solving needed to get there. Really take the time to do dry runs and dive into edge cases. Basically, the step by step process that we covered in the coding module.

title: My personal Experience as Frontend Developer
content:
I wanted to share an honest observation and get feedback from others especially those with a frontend background.

When I joined the program it was presented as being for engineers with different backgrounds which I really appreciated. I also understand that this approach has helped many people so this feedback is more about alignment with individual goals rather than criticism.
I have about four years of frontend experience and in the videos it is mentioned that we should apply for roles we are qualified for. Based on that I have been applying to frontend roles and have been getting interviews. In those interviews the questions have focused on the following:

• DOM manipulation and event handling
• Building React forms with validation and error handling
• State management and controlled components
• Implementing pagination
• Optimizing data rendering and performance

One challenge I have personally faced is the requirement to complete 20 mandatory LeetCode questions. While I understand the value of DSA practice for my goals this has felt somewhat unbalanced for frontend preparation. I would personally benefit more from a blended approach for example 10 LeetCode questions paired with 10 frontend focused problems such as GreatFrontend exercises that better reflect how frontend interviews are conducted.

Right now the heavier emphasis on LeetCode and Python based problem solving has taken time away from deepening core frontend skills like React TypeScript Tailwind Redux and DOM fundamentals which are the areas being tested most often in the interviews I am getting.

I am curious how other frontend focused engineers are approaching this:
• Have you adjusted the LeetCode requirement to better fit frontend goals
• Is there flexibility in balancing DSA practice with frontend specific interview preparation
• Has anyone successfully combined frontend practice resources alongside the program structure

I am sharing this as constructive feedback and with the intent of getting the most value out of the program while staying aligned with the roles I am pursuing.

title: Advice on Technical Interview Preparation (Amplitude)
content:
Hi everyone, Happy New Year! <3 :\)

I hope you all had a wonderful holiday season.

I recently completed a HackerRank round for a Software Engineer role at Amplitude and had a phone screening afterward. During the call, the recruiter mentioned that the next round would likely involve an extension of the HackerRank question.

**The problem was a schema-validation task where a list of employees is validated against a schema defining required fields, allowed fields, and field types. It also supports nested employees using array:employee, making the solution recursive. The validation returns the first error based on priority: missing required fields, then type mismatches, and finally unexpected properties.**

I wanted to kindly ask for your guidance on what extensions or follow-up questions are commonly asked in such rounds. Would you recommend focusing more on extending this problem \(edge cases, scalability, design improvements\), or should I continue with regular LeetCode practice alongside it?

Any advice or suggestions would be greatly appreciated.Thank you so much for your time and help.

title: T1 Quant (HRT) Technical Interview Tips!
content:
Small win - interviewing with **Hudson River Trading** for Algo Dev role next, next Friday.

It's a role bridging core dev \(C++ infra, OS, low-level optimizations\), and researchers \(hypothesizing ideas with Jupyter, ML, probstat, complex math modeling\). I think they \(hopefully we\) will be doing a bit of both.

Planning to study \(priority descending as per interview procedure required - learning on the go - list is comprehensive! meaning no more will be packed in\):
[ul][li]Probstat: Combinatorics -> Bayes -> Distributions -> EV / other foundational stats -> CLT -> Markov Chains \(Markov is the only advanced probstat concept, so no Martingale walk, no stochatic calculus\)[li]Python: memory management \(reference counting vs garbage collection\), concurrency libraries - both theory and implementation \(Multithreading, Multiprocessing, Asyncio\)[li]OS: virtualization and concurrency[li]C++: smart pointers, rvalue references, move semantics, lambdas... \(this is the only incomplete one since my cpp experience is limited, may edit later\)

Question is, how do I take it a step further beyond the theory! Here is what I found online someone wrote a few years back who were in the exact same shoes as me:

"...The first round was a probability question. Although they sent a CoderPad link via email, it was mainly used to run simulations for the probability-related problems. The second round was the actual live coding.

The problem setup: We're a trading company that receives a profit X_t each day, where t is the time index. We're considering n days, so from X_1 to X_n. We're interested in the average return, and the question is, what metric would be better to use? If you had to choose only one between mean and median, which one would you pick?

Then they gave a specific scenario: With probability 0.2, we set X = μ; with probability 0.8, we set X ~ N\(μ, 1\). In this case, is it better to use the mean or the median to estimate μ? You can use NumPy in CoderPad to simulate it.

title: Sharing
content:
Happy New Years All,
I built a tool for myself and I want to share in case others feel the same as me...

I feel like all lists I've made for myself on Excel or Bookmarks end up causing the same problem.

When I do the problems in the same order I don't have to "shift gears" to understand the problem deeply and can solve from muscle memory, having just solved an simpler variation of the problem via solving a previous problem in the same category/list.

The crux of this tool is to allow us the user to filter for problems\(difficulty/category/list\) and then randomly sort the filtered problems. In this way I feel like it's helped me to be able to master the core skills because again, I'm not just remembering "after house robber where I use a recursive top down memo I have house robber ii in my list, which is doing the same thing except I clip the front & back of the list and return that the max of those".

Put another way:

I find it helpful to do problems in the same category. I just need to do them in random order so that I'm actively contemplating "should I use an adjacency matrix vs adjacency list" instead of "doing the same algorithm as the previous problem with x twist".

I hope that makes sense... lol.

[https://loi-tran-blog.netlify.app/dsa](https://loi-tran-blog.netlify.app/dsa)

title: AI Prompt to generate resume bullet points
content:
Hi all,

To really maximize the bullet points on my resume, I used AI \(ex. ChatGPT, Claude\) and the ideas presented in the “Write a Top 1% Resume” module. Here is the prompt I used:

\[fill in the blank\] = anything in square brackets is for you to fill out
```
I am using Jake's resume and writing bullet points for my work experience. Each experience should have 3-5 bullets, each of those bullets should be multi-lined \(2 lines\), using up the full 2 lines \(it will come out to 198 characters\). Include periods at the end of each bullet point. It should be in this format "Action verb, main accomplishment…, so that…, which means…, resulting in…" and it should have some kind of metric.

Examples of metrics.
■ % Improvement
■ 10x \(times change\)

title: Anduril and LinkedIn Offers!
content:
Hi everyone, I’ve been part of the program since August and wanted to share some wins at the end of my recruiting season. I received SWE internship offers from Anduril and LinkedIn, with the LinkedIn offer specifically in systems and infrastructure. Anduril is paying $50/hour, while LinkedIn is paying $70/hour. Both offer free transportation, food, and housing. I haven’t made a decision yet, so I’d love to hear others’ opinions.

I also wanted to reflect on how the program helped me throughout recruiting. I’ve detailed the process for every company I interviewed with below, so there should be a lot of useful information there.

There were two major ways the program helped me. As a Master’s student with four years of undergrad behind me, I had significant experience preparing for and doing behavioral interviews, but much less experience with technical interviews. I’d been doing LeetCode for years, but had never done a real LC interview before this semester. Doing mock interviews with [@Nikhil Hegde](obj://user/5f7f9e011863414c96fc6141fb0cf23a) was a wake-up call—I realized I was severely underprepared for the real thing. I immediately started timing my problem-solving speed and focused more on clearly talking through my approach. The mocks ended up being perfect preparation for actual interviews.

The second major help was learning how to reach out for referrals. I believe about half of my interviews came from referrals. Even though I didn’t get that many, they tremendously boosted my interview rate. It’s genuinely worth sending hundreds of requests—when they work out, the payoff is huge.

One final note is the discrepancy between interviews I received while at UGA versus UPenn. My resume didn’t change much, yet while at UGA I never received a big-tech or FAANG-level interview. As you’ll see below, I think the UPenn name brand made a massive difference.

Interviews
Google
One OA after getting referred, followed by two coding problems. Both were medium-to-hard LeetCode difficulty. I solved both, but in the second round I used an O\(nlogn\) solution, which was the “medium” approach. The interviewer wanted an O\(n\) solution, which I believe was the “hard” version, so I received a tiebreaker round. In that round, I almost immediately found the solution and explained it, but my interviewer didn’t seem convinced and ended up walking through the entire solution themselves. Despite solving it correctly, I received a rejection.

title: 🚀 The Power of the Second Ask: Overcoming Job Search Shame
content:
Before joining the Accelerator, I had a great opportunity: a referral from my very successful cousin, who works at Microsoft, for a Software Engineering role.

To my shock, Microsoft still ghosted even with the referral.

The shame was real. Based on the incredible \(and necessary\) constructive criticism I’ve received here, I know now that my resume simply wasn't reflecting my true value. But at the time, all I felt was the fear of disappointing my cousin. I was convinced he would be embarrassed that Microsoft didn't even respond to his referral.

It took overcoming that shame and discomfort—something the accelerator explicitly forced me to do—to try again. I cooked up the courage to reach out to him and ask for a referral once more, and his response was everything: he told me he would refer me "70x7 times"!

This is my reminder to everyone here: There is no shame in being rejected, ghosted, or needing to re-apply. Our field is competitive, and sometimes the only thing standing between you and the job is a more optimized resume or a better approach.

Don't let one failure prevent you from making the second ask. Get back up, refine your materials, and try once more. Your network is there to support your effort, not condemn your setbacks.

title: Bittersweet Win
content:
Hi everyone, today I locked in a founding engineer role at an HF0-backed startup. I've always wanted to write a big “wins” post here to cheer you guys up, but my feelings are currently quite complicated and bittersweet, so I wanted to make a reflection post instead.

The last few months were rough. I followed the playbooks, grinded referrals, and still took some hilarious L’s:
[ul][li]Spent weeks getting a director-level referral at Riot Games only to fail the OA[li]Passed all rounds and got a verbal offer from ByteDance’s top AI team, then had to turn it down myself because of CPT issues. I felt like my entire world collapsed and I couldn't even go to school the next day.

Then everything flipped by accident.

I went to a Halloween hacker house party the company hosted. Somehow I was the only person who showed up, so I had to raw-dog a 4 hour conversation with the whole team about AI \(there were probably toe-scratch marks on the floor by the end\). I watched them work for a bit, they were working on intent-parsing LLMs, and I opened my laptop and wrote them a 200-example auto-eval diagnostic to help them improve accuracy.

They asked me to come back the next day and I've been rolling with them ever since.

The wild part: an HF0 startup somehow had nobody familiar with synthetic data generation. I happened to know it. They needed it. That was it. After months of grinding LeetCode, interviews, and rejections… I got my best offer by going to a random party where no-one else showed up.

Life feels unreal. I lost my “dream internship,” lost a FAANG offer, and ended up with something better than both.

I wish I had a clean, sharable “method” for everyone here, but honestly the only two pieces of advice that feel true are:
[ul][li]Live in SF[li]Go to SF events in person

But I know those aren’t practical for 95% of people.

Here's my rule of thumb for going to events. The event is worth going to if:
[ul][li]You're going cause you get to talk to people \(hacker houses, mixers, networking events\). [li]You're not going cause you can hear someone else talk \(tech talks or hackathons you don't have a chance of winning\).

title: Not a major win, but maybe a 'minor win'?
content:
Recently, Cognizant Canada launched their "Cognizant Skills Accelerator’s GenAI Pathway". I applied for the program by submitting my updated resume through a warm referral, and a few days later, I received an invitation to participate in a 30 minute screening process.

The first 15 minutes were dedicated to answering 15 multiple-choice questions on general Python concepts. After that, I faced a coding challenge—a LeetCode-style Easy-Medium problem. The catch was that I had to solve it within a tight 15-minute timer. It was challenging under the time pressure, but I managed to complete it successfully.

Yesterday, I received an email informing me that I’m one of the few candidates shortlisted for the program. This initiative provides an opportunity to connect with industry leaders at Cognizant, earn a digital badge that can be shared on LinkedIn, and potentially be considered for employment. While a job offer isn’t guaranteed, the fact that they’re conducting a screening process and offering a seven-week program for free suggests that hiring a select few might be their ultimate goal. The program starts from 24th Jan 2025.

Regardless of the outcome, the program offers numerous benefits—it’s free, provides valuable learning opportunities, grants a credential I can share, enables networking with professionals, and opens up the possibility of employment. With all these positives, I see no downside in putting in the effort. It’s been less than a month since my start date, and I’m already seeing progress. title: CEO of Xerox | Just a Quick Point on Referrals
content:
I used to think networking meant going to hackathons or messaging CTOs on Twitter.
I was wrong \(this Accelerator has taught me\). The best lead I’ve gotten in my entire job search \(just 3 weeks into the Accelerator tomorrow\) didn't come from GitHub or LinkedIn. It came from my mom’s church.

Here is what happened:
[ol:1][li]My mom knows [the CEO of Xerox](https://www.linkedin.com/in/steven-bandrowczak-51866a4/) through her church community.[li]She mentioned I was looking for work.[li]He connected me directly to the Head of Talent Acquisition.[li]I now have a meeting booked with the hiring manager.

The Takeaway: If I hadn't exhausted my personal connections—even the ones that seem totally unrelated to software engineering—I would still be just another resume in the pile.
If you are struggling to get interviews, stop looking out there for a second and look at your existing circle. Your aunt, your pastor, or your neighbor might be one degree of separation away from your next boss.

Now it's up to me to crush the interview, but the door is open.

title: Sharing my Job Search & LinkedIn Automation Setup
content:
Hey there!

[@Yvonne Wang](obj://user/1d66bc8d93824f2f8dca9652eb30da53) asked me to share my job search/Linkedin automation and my super simple Job/Referral tracker with you all, I hated doing it. So just tried to remove the friction. Hopefully it helps!

To being with you would need perplexity premium, which is free for a year for anyone with a valid student email. You can use this link [https://pplx.ai/ast1044](https://pplx.ai/ast1044).

Prompt#1 to find job posted in the last 72 hrs for new grads withing 2hrs of the GTA\(Greater Toronto Area\).
`Search for top 3 companies located in the Greater Toronto Area or within a 2-hour driving radius of Toronto \(including Guelph, Kitchener, London, Ottawa\) that are currently hiring junior or new grad software developers. Only include postings from the last 3 days. Return the company name, job title, location, LinkedIn job link, and the official company website link if available.`

Prompt#2 to verify those jobs are valid by checking the company’s website
`For the below companies hiring junior or new grad software developers in the Greater Toronto Area or nearby cities, then for each, check their official careers page to confirm if the role listed on LinkedIn is still posted there. title: Capital One Senior SWE Power Day Experience and Breakdown
content:
Hey everyone,

I passed my Capital One Power Day for a Senior Software Engineer role and wanted to share my experience! I'm making this extremely detailed, so bear with me!

The interview process was straightforward and easy since I've done ~400 LeetCode problems over the last several months. \(I also had a resource for leaked questions, it's Google-able, but I can share it if it's allowed!\). From what I've heard, this interview is similar for mid to senior engineers. Juniors/interns may or may not have more difficult coding problems.

[ul][li]Typically the first interview will be the coding round and they will ask you a question like Simple Bank System from LeetCode and extend it to ask for the "Top K bank accounts" by some criteria \(hint: heaps!\). If it's not this question, it will be some variation of the top asked questions in the Capital One LeetCode tag. Just make sure you know heaps, hashmaps, intervals, sliding window, binary search, and basic array traversal and you should be good. I don't think Capital One asks graphs or trees, but if they do, God help you because the company tagged questions are rough for those. 🤣[li]The next interview will be system design of some relevant banking concept, like a credit card application system \(what I got\), a customer-facing chatbot, or loan system. You don't have to know these systems in depth, but just follow the requirements and you can make logical inferences. Also, ASK QUESTIONS. I asked SO many questions to the point where the interviewers would tell me that I could stop because I was getting too in the weeds for what they wanted. But doing so helped me know what they were expecting and how in depth they wanted me to go. They won't push you on concepts you don't know about, but if you mention a Kafka message queue, for example, they expect you to know why you chose it and that you didn't just regurgitate it from ChatGPT.[li]Next is behavioral. I suck at talking about myself, so if you're good at these, you'll be good. Specifically for mid to senior levels, they want to know how you're involved cross-functionally with other non-engineering coworkers and how you factor in the overall business when making decisions, and interacting with stakeholders. I interact with people from various departments on a regular basis during projects, so this was easy for me to bring up. They will press you for more details, so know what you're talking about and also don't sound like you regurgitated a response from ChatGPT.[li]Finally is the case study round, where they will give you a prompt for a system like a virtual credit card system and you have to first understand how it works and make simple calculations based on that information. Then from there, they will give you some small code snippet to debug. You're expected to know what it does, where the error is, and fix it. Then the last part is an extension to the original criteria and then you fix the code snippet to account for that. Apparently most people don't finish that part, so it's optional. At least finish the parts before that to pass.

title: DON'T WAIT!! -- Schedule Your Mock Technical Interview!
content:
Hi! Just a quick reminder to schedule your mock coding interviews during your two-month period and to not wait until you have a real interview coming up. The goal is to build your foundation early so you’re always ready, rather than cramming under pressure later on.

By starting now, you’ll be prepared, confident, and ready to go when that interview invite comes—rather than scrambling to practice in the final days before it. This applies to both behavioral and technical interviews!

Even if you haven’t mastered LeetCode yet, mock interviews are incredibly valuable—they highlight areas to improve and help you build confidence over time.
Technical interviews aren’t just about writing code. Interviewers are also evaluating:
[ul][li]Logical thinking[li]Communication skills[li]Decision-making and analysis

And unlike coding itself, these soft skills aren’t as easily trainable through LeetCode. They improve through practice in real interview settings, where you’re asked to explain your thought process, break down problems out loud, and respond to questions on the spot. That’s exactly what mock interviews are for.

I’ll be here to provide feedback on what you’re doing well and where you can improve—and to help you get past those first technical interview jitters!

Let me know if you have any questions or want help prepping!

Link to schedule a mock technical interview \(LeetCode/System Design\): [https://calendly.com/software-engineering-accelerator/coding-interview?preview_source=et_card](https://calendly.com/software-engineering-accelerator/coding-interview?preview_source=et_card)

title: Unsure how to proceed from here
content:
For some context, I started the program in the beginning of July before the recruiting season officially started. I got a lot of "guaranteed" referrals beforehand, as in I have gone on phone calls and had people agree to refer me. However, since its been so long a lot of them ended up not responding to my requests when the job opened up. That or even if someone did agree to refer me once the job opened up, it would often close before I even get a chance to get their referral.

I have had some OA's and a few interviews, but the interviews were mainly from career fairs at my school.

As of last month I began to mainly prioritize applying early as I heard from many different sources that that will give you the best shot. So far I am around 70-100 applications in \(with ~20 referrals\) and I am not really sure which direction to go. I try to apply to around 5-7 jobs per day but its been a bit inconsistent lately. So naturally I thought of applying first then immediately afterward asking for a referral, but then almost all the time the referral only counts during the application not afterward. That also then raises the question of what will be more valuable: being one of the first 100 to apply or having a referral a few days later \(assuming you withdraw the earlier app so it won't flag the system\)?

Since I know there is still a lot of time to make things right, I want to know what will give me the best shot. I am a college sophomore applying for SWE internships for next year.

title: Harsh lesson I learned. Has this happened to y’all?
content:
Ok, so I was going to post a win, but it turned into an L real quick. This is also somewhat of a vent, but don’t make the same mistake I made.

So I went to my school’s Career Fair, the UC Irvine STEM career fair, and I talked to many companies, most were impressed with my resume and took my resume and exchanged LinkedIn/emails, etc. I asked for recruiter emails and all that.

Ok, so for the weird part, I talked to Arista Networks and immediately noticed they were being selective on whose resume they were taking. And they had a special QR code for applying. I was one of the people they took a resume from, so I felt good about that.

However, this is where I should have been more proactive I was going to wait till the end of the day, after the fair and all my classes, to do all the follow-up emails/LinkedIn messages/ and applications.

However, during one of my courses after the fair, I received a recruiter email that I didn’t check until an hour later, which screwed me over, and it was the Arista Networks recruiter asking me to apply for the position, so he could offer me an interview because my resume wasn’t in the system yet. So I applied immediately after I noticed it, and he sent me the link to set up an appointment. However, when I checked it, all appointment times were filled. And when I asked the recruiter, he said that I’d have to wait till if/when more internships pop up. He said he’d contact me then.

I just can’t believe I screwed myself over. Very harsh lesson I learned:

[ol:1][li]Apply then and there, the moment you scan the QR code, DON'T wait till the end of the day.[li]Check your emails religiously, exempt them from your Do Not Disturb if you have to. An hour late response can cost you dearly.

Has this happened to you? Where a company gave interviews on a first-come first-serve basis? This just seems really weird. I thought most companies have a dedicated number of people they email and a certain number of interview spots. Really weird. Plus, several hours right after the fair, I’ve never heard of that, the rest of the companies said they’d get back to me within the next week or month. So the same day just blew past my mind. I mean, at least the next day, maybe, this was a first, I thought on the spot interviews or "campus interviews" died many years ago.

title: How do you talk about AI tool usage in interviews?
content:
I am curious how to navigate the topic of generative AI use in the development process when it comes to interviews, your resume, and generally marketing yourself. AI tools are still relatively new and there are varying opinions about how they should be used and how often they should be used. However, this seems to be a somewhat controversial topic, with some companies looking for you to be comfortable using generative AI extensively as a necessity, and others viewing that kind of use as a red flag.

I'm personally interested in this topic in the context of early-career and internship hiring, although I recognize others in the program at different career stages likely have similar questions. The reason I find this particularly salient when looking for internships is that if you're a student or otherwise early in your SWE career, you don't have as much experience/knowledge, and use of generative AI has the risk of replacing valuable learning opportunities afforded by tackling problems on your own.

In my day-to-day development workflow and learning, I'm careful to use tools like Claude in a way that still challenges me to think through the problem at hand—by having it ask me leading questions rather than directly solving the problem for me or automatically generating a bunch of code. If I need to seed a database with a bunch of sample data, then absolutely I'm going to pass that on to Claude.

Given this view, this is the genuine answer I would give if someone asked how I utilize AI in the development process. However, I also recognize that many companies are now looking for people that can leverage AI tools to their fullest extent to accelerate development as productivity expectations are rapidly rising.

I would love to hear everyone's thoughts on:
[ul][li]How is gen AI usage in tech perceived at different companies you've worked with or interviewed at?[li]Have you found effective ways to discuss your AI workflow in interviews?[li]For those doing hiring: what distinguishes thoughtful AI usage from over-reliance?[li]Should the topic be avoided if you are applying for interships/early-career?

title: Get Your Foot in the Door
content: Just a tip for those seeking full-time employment, consider similar tech roles, not strictly software engineering. For example, at Salesforce there’s a role called Forward Deployed Engineer with a much easier interview process than SWE, yet it still pays very well \(base salary $125,700–$334,600, not including annual bonuses or RSUs\). Once you’re in, if you perform well, even just decently, you can network with other employees and hiring managers to switch roles if that’s your goal. We strongly prioritize internal applicants, specially those who have proven to be top performers. And if you do switch, you’ll bring years of domain specific knowledge and a strong internal network across different teams and roles. I've referred a ton of people so I'm not sure if I'm going to hit a limit, but I'm willing to find out what that limit is. Feel free to connect with me via LinkedIn: [https://www.linkedin.com/in/kevingreenb1/](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kevingreenb1/)

title: Use AlgoMonster before doing a new LeetCode Concept (3-Steps)
content:
Hey everyone 👋 I wanted to share a little system I’ve been using to learn new coding concepts before jumping into LeetCode. It’s been super helpful for me, so maybe it’ll help you too.
Here’s what I do:

1. Start with AlgoMonster 👉 [https://algo.monster/templates](https://algo.monster/templates)

[ul][li]Pick the topic you want to learn from the left sidebar.[li]Read their free articles — they do a great job explaining the concepts and giving examples.[li]Pay extra attention to their animated diagrams. Seriously, these are gold. Watch them a couple of times until you really see how the data is moving around.

2. Use their coding templates

[ul][li]Go back to the template page \([https://algo.monster/templates](https://algo.monster/templates)\)[li]Choose your programming language \(top right\).[li]Select the concept you’re working on.[li]You’ll get a ready-made coding template. DO NOT copy-paste it. Instead, study it closely. [li]Walk through it line by line until you understand how the code manipulates the data.

3. Put it into practice right away

[ul][li]As soon as you finish the first two steps, head over to LeetCode.[li]Try at least one easy problem related to the concept. Two is even better.[li]This locks the idea in your brain because you’re applying it immediately.

That’s it! Simple, repeatable, and \(at least for me\) a lot less overwhelming than jumping straight into problems without really “getting” the concept first. Let me know what you think of this strategy.

title: Failed xAI Interview, Want to Go Over It While I Remember
content:
Hey everyone, failed my XAI interview on CodeSignal.

It was a matrix manipulation problem that involved falling blocks.

- : skip
% : box
* : bomb

Then some matrix:

\[ -, -, %, *\],
\[%, - , -, *\],
\[*, %, %, -\]

The box would fall down a column on every iteration.

If it hit a bomb it would explode clearing 8 spaces around it.

Boxes also stacked once they reached the bottom.

It was actually pretty simple, and I believe that I would’ve been able to finish it if I had more time, but I spent too much time trying to find the index and value of the boxes and bombs. Which is super disappointing because that’s pretty much the easiest part!

The harder part was the matrix manipulation, and creating the proper rules to make sure the boxes moved properly.

Does anyone have some time to go over this problem with me? I have lost hundreds of thousands of dollars in opportunities because I can’t code fast enough and I’m really upset about it!

title: Experience Alchemy Opportunity
content:
I wanted to share something with you all:

I just got done doing a technical interview for a research lab at my university. It's called the UGA small satellite research lab, and they were recruiting students for SWE positions. Could be a really cool opportunity and could sound very unique on a resume since most SWE jobs don't involve low-level C++ programming of literally satellites.

It was 45 minutes long, and I was given 4 leetcode problems \(only because I was fast at solving them, I would have been given less if I was slower\):

[ul][li]Given two sorted arrays, combine into one sorted array \(really easy warm up\)[li]Valid Parenthesis \(stack question\)[li]Count of smaller numbers after self \(major curveball, could only implement brute force\)[li]Kth largest element in an array \(Heap\)

Overall I feel good about this interview: I felt my interviewers were impressed by my skills and communication skills. #315 Count of smaller numbers after self has an optimal O\(n\(log\(n\)\)\) solution that I couldn't quite figure out, but the interviewers themselves couldn't even explain it, and it is a hard difficulty question so surely not getting it optimally won't kill my chances. I had no problem solving the others.

If I land this, I could market this a 1+ year experience on my resume before I even graduate, which could be huge, and even huge for my current 2026 SWE internship hunt.

Wish me luck!

title: One Application vs. Multiple Applications
content:
"If I just submit a million applications, one of them has to stick, right?" 😂

I'm about to spill some juicy secrets about the Applicant Tracking Systems \(ATS\)! 🤫

The magic number is - one to two strong application per company at a time, max!

[ul][li]Anything more than 1-2 applications per company will cause problems.[li]Recruiters will have to sift through all the different roles you've applied for, trying to figure out what you're actually qualified for.[li]If they do want to move you to the next step, they'll have to coordinate with other recruiters to understand the status of your other applications.[li]This added complexity can slow down the process or cause them to move on to the next candidate instead.

So lesson here is to be "strategic and selective" with your applications.

[ul][li]Only apply to jobs you're truly qualified. Pay close attention to minimum qualifications on the job description [li]Tailor your application! [li]Don't waste time and energy on roles you're not qualified for - it'll just hurt your chances

Hope this was helpful for all of you that are ready to land those AMAZING tech careers. 🚀 I'm hosting my office hours every Wednesday 3:00pm PST Via [Zoom](https://us06web.zoom.us/meeting/register/rPeImaixQjmT82vjUnljYw). Feel free to register and come and hang out with me.

title: Joined the 100 problem club!
content:
Hey everyone, I'm excited to share that I just completed my 100th problem, and my first hard! This was no easy journey: I'm sure many of you are way past this level but I made it my mission to prioritize challenging problems and more importantly: focused on fully understanding why the solution works. By asking AI questions whenever I got stuck, the learning process was even more valuable to me.

Although some OA's like Roblox, TikTok, and Capital One tripped me up, sub-FAANG level OA's from Cisco, Wells Fargo, and BlackRock were super easy for me. One thing I've noticed is that OA problems tend to me more string manipulation, 1D and 2D arrays, math, and language fluency testing rather than DSA/pareto problem set problems, so my advice to all of you is to spend extra time on the "annoying" string problems on leetcode as they were my biggest pitfall on these OAs. I'll definitely be spending more time on these types of problems before I attempt my JPMorgan Chase and Shopify OA.

To anyone struggling with leetcode: You are not alone. Keep grinding. There were way more hours put into these 100 problems than I can even remember, and leetcode only gets easier the more and more problems you've done. Good luck!

UPDATE: I unfortunately failed the Shopify OA and got rejected, but I completed the JPMorgan Chase OA in only 20 minutes despite having an hour!

title: What to do when I hit a wall in the program?

title: 4 days to prep for Uber interview, any tips?
content:
Hi there,

I only have 4 days to prepare for Uber’s 60 min technical interview. The opportunity came all of a sudden \(really grateful\) and they are hiring within the next month which is the reason for the short notice interview. I want to maximize my limited time.

This is for a mobile entry level role \(iOS and Android\). Here's the interview structure:
[ul][li]Coding exercises - 45 minutes[li]Design & Architecture - 15 minutes \(You may be asked to walk through a past project, highlighting your approach to problem-solving, design decisions, and collaboration - especially within the scope of your own contributions.\)

Here are some sample topics they’ve provided:
[ul][li]Coding: construct/traverse data structures, implement system routines, distill large data sets to single values, transform one data set to another.[li]Algorithm Design / Analysis: big-O analysis, sorting and hashing, handling obscenely large amounts of data.[li]Open-Ended Discussion: biggest challenges faced, best/worst designs seen, performance analysis and optimization, testing, ideas for improving existing products.

Here are resources they have provided me:
[ul][li][Software Developer Interview Prep](https://tracking.icims.com/f/a/27tPFgpENydmeuge-eg2gQ~~/AAIB5hA~/FnU0w7Wl6q99TaNdXsyIqRDFGiCxQ3gVGR4z7pSHwK-mILFEFKroLfxq9cqjkLt-hLyRIRNt89I6Fn0PkK-7u4HLHT0eyNgUFtc6zrrU8FlST-UtNkaJw9uhD9hNMbegQhnZDGYLafAtJhT5zvYlPA~~)[li][Topcoder](https://tracking.icims.com/f/a/X1-Ia0eJdI_ylgsqxBUX9w~~/AAIB5hA~/Mk_gVHFWErTPl9sZmucMHZ8pX3-YlZdbNyekE0b0XXRKhQ2xJwZUZNQ4LXLO76KENpraVq-KdEvnShWCXZM03-v0sQuKHXMhNlOPYwMwJKk~) - Launch the "Arena" widget and then go to the practice rooms to solve problems.[li][Projecteuler.net](http://Projecteuler.net)[li][Eng.uber.com](http://Eng.uber.com) -- Learn more about the technology behind Uber Engineering[li][Uber.com/community/](http://Uber.com/community/) -- Learn more about Uber's culture, leaders, offerings, and so much more.[li]The Algorithm Design Manual by Steven Skiena [li]Cracking the Coding Interview by Gayle McDowell

title: Startup CEO reached out — should I accept?
content:
A startup CEO recently contacted me regarding a potential opportunity to join his company. After reviewing the startup, which launched earlier this year, I found the concept intriguing and subsequently sent over my resume. The CEO responded and offered me an internship as a Software Developer. However, the position is currently unpaid: "the internship will be unpaid for a while until we become profitable or receive an investment from angels or venture capital. Currently, our interns are getting paid in equity \(shares\)."

While I’m not specifically looking for unpaid internships, I’m considering this opportunity because I believe the additional experience could strengthen my resume and improve my chances of landing a paid internship next summer. For context, my current experience is primarily with startup projects alongside peers.

Should I accept this offer?

Here are the pros and cons I’ve identified:

Pros
[ol:1][li]Gain additional real-world experience in a startup environment[li]Opportunity to learn and work with Swift/Kotlin[li]Hands-on experience collaborating within a larger team \(6 members\)[li]Potential to receive equity if the startup succeeds

Cons
[ol:1][li]Investing time in an early-stage, unproven startup rather than seeking opportunities at more established companies[li]Unpaid position, with compensation only in the form of equity \(which may ultimately have no value\)[li]The experience may not have as significant an impact on my resume as I hope

title: Honest Question: How do you tell people that you are a part of the Accelerator school?
content:

I had an honest question for the community: Does anyone get embarrassed to admit that they needed a paid program to land a software engineering job...that we couldn't do it on our own? How do you approach telling people, or do you just say you are grinding the job application process?

This program - Aman's perfected structure, the coaches' talent and expertise, and it's collaborative community - are undoubtedly amazing and successful. But for some reason, I get self-conscious and I kinda feel privileged if I admit that I'm doing this.

[ol:1][li]You have the right to share as much or as little as you want with people - so just don't mention it to people who won't understand why this program is necessary to achieve your goals.[li]Show them one of Aman's YouTube videos and they'll probably see the vision lol[li]Tell them upfront that you are joining an accelerator program to prepare yourself for the job search, no need to mention the cost or anything, but hopefully they'll see how hard you are working

title: How I Secure Referrals + Get Their Phone Numbers
content:
LinkedIn DMs and email can be slow. The best contact info you can get from a referral is their phone number.

Here’s how I do it naturally through my coffee chat workflow:

Calendly Setup:
I use Calendly to book coffee chats and set it up to collect phone numbers as part of the scheduling form.

10 Min Before the Chat:
I send a quick text: “Hey \[Name\], excited to chat! I’ll be in the call — hop in whenever you’re ready. No rush.”Just a friendly nudge that shows you're prepared and chill.

During the Chat:
I casually say: “Oh, I realized I texted you without asking — hope that was okay!”Most people say something like “Yeah no worries” — and now it’s normal to text them.

After Getting the Referral:
I ask: “Would it be okay if I text you when the application opens? These roles fill up quick, and I just want to give myself the best shot. Would make it easier for you too.”
It’s polite, practical, and shows respect for their time.

This approach has worked really well for me. It keeps the vibe respectful and human while also building a more reliable line of contact that they will actually check. Calendly takes about 30min to hour to fully setup, but I use it almost everyday now.

title: Linkedin Tip for Bootcamp Grads or non-trad (Aman asked me to post this)
content:
I've been chatting with a few members from non-traditional paths \(like bootcamp grads\), and one challenge that keeps coming up is:

“How do I find good people to connect with on LinkedIn when I don’t have a university network?”

One thing I suggested that's worked for me so far is this:

🎯 Research a few well-known bootcamps \(like App Academy, Hack Reactor, Flatiron, General Assembly, etc.\) and use those names as search filters on LinkedIn.

Once you connect with a few bootcamp grads, it gets easier when you search "\[bootcamp\] software engineer" + Filters \(company, position, location\) —LinkedIn will start surfacing more mutuals from their cohorts, which helps filter out the noise and makes outreach feel a lot more natural.

Also wanted to share a talking point that’s come up a lot in my coffee chats with bootcamp grads:

I always mention how I genuinely admire their journey. I tell them I can’t imagine how hard it must’ve been to break into tech without the safety net of a university, and how I would’ve been extremely anxious in their position. That usually opens up a really honest and helpful convo—people appreciate when you meet them with respect and empathy.

Some of the most valuable referrals and convos I’ve had came from these.

title: Resume + LinkedIn Review #3 and General Questions
content:

Technical Skills & Job Applications:

Should I continue applying to jobs requiring languages I haven't used recently, even though I can learn quickly with AI assistance?"
2. Multiple Resume Strategy: "Would it be effective to create multiple master resumes tailored for different role categories: development, QA, support, DevOps, analysis, or technical sales? Or should I stick with one versatile version?"

How do I position my adaptability as a strength rather than uncertainty, especially at 26 without my first paid tech position? Will recruiters likely have similar concerns?"

title: Update: Coffee Chat with Start-up Founder
content:
First, I would like to thank all the coaches who replied. Their advice was helpful in preparing as best as possible for this introductory chat.

I believe the chat went well, right off the bat, he said he was giving me an opportunity since we both attend the same University. I did my research on the startup, understood their product, target clients, founder vision, even competitors, etc. So I was prepared to ask insightful questions.

title: Recruiter Tip | Focus on Improving your Technical Writing
content:
✍️Documentation skills are a crucial component of being an effective engineering team member.

Beyond technical expertise in Software Engineering ~ you must demonstrate the ability to clearly document processes and workflows. On top of Leet Code Online Assessments for certain technical roles, there will be an additional Writing Sample Assessment which requires you to describe and write a process change, product idea, or new metric/new interface.

This includes:
[ol:1][li]Accurately capturing technical procedures | Document Project Implementations | Trouble shooting guides | Technical Specifications and User Playbook [li]Using appropriate industry terminology and not assuming everyone understands acronyms the[li]Understanding and conveying in an easy to understand format [li]Writing clear, accessible descriptions that allow readers \(non technical stakeholders to fully comprehend complex situations[li]Strong documentation ensures knowledge sharing across the team and creates a valuable reference for current and future team members. Your ability to communicate technical concepts in writing is just as important as your hands-on engineering work. 

⭐KEY- Focus on how you can make the most complex concepts accessible to promote the transparent communication across cross functional stakeholders

While pursuing new projects and certifications is valuable for career growth, I encourage everyone in this community to begin developing strong technical writing skills and how to leverage AI in this space to help you with efficiency and productivity.

title: Job Site Recommendation for Startups
content:
After starting my internship, I came across [Communitech’s job board](https://www1.communitech.ca/jobs), which I found super helpful—especially since the startup I work for is also part of their network.

This platform focuses on startup opportunities and lets you filter by company size, job type, and experience level. It’s backed by the Government of Canada, so most of the listings are legitimate and not scams. While startups can always carry some risk, many on this site are backed by solid VC funding \(e.g. Y Combinator\).

If you’re looking for a way to get started, I highly recommend browsing the [company directory](https://www1.communitech.ca/companies) to find startups you're interested in. A good strategy is to reach out directly to the CTO or CEO on LinkedIn—especially if the company has under 100 employees.

Pro tip: Mention that you’re open to unpaid work to get your foot in the door. That said, unpaid internships are technically illegal in Canada unless they’re part of a formal education program. So in most cases, companies will pay you something— just to avoid legal risk.

title: Scale AI Offer
content:
$50/hr SF + benefits. Excited to be a Scalien.

Three tips that will help you land the internship: 1. Mentality 2. Consistency 3. Environment

This is a reflection of what's worked for me.

1.
All of you already know how much you want the internships. You have the resilience to keep trying, even through rejection, that's the reason you're on Skool right now. You also have the belief in yourself that you are qualified to get the job. Also, as Andrej Karpathy says, you cannot compare yourself with others.

I struggled with understanding and ingraining in my mind had that no one's gonna help you during the interviews or oas it's only you. So acting independently, ethically, and diligently is a must.

Showing up every day is a massive multiplier for you. I was able to get two jobs in three weeks sporadically after always taking action. 1% improvement daily is 1.01^365 = 38x better. title: Are Interns Worth Reaching Out To for Referrals or Connections?
content:
When reaching out to people at companies I’m targeting, I’ve noticed interns or ex-interns are usually the most responsive. But I’m not sure if it’s worth the effort — can they even refer someone? And if not, should I still try to connect in hopes of getting pointed to a recruiter or hiring manager?
What I’m thinking:
[ul][li]Still reach out to interns/ex-interns — they might not be able to refer, but they could offer great advice or help connect me with someone who can.[li]Skip interns and aim for full-time engineers or recruiters instead, since they’re more likely to have referral power.[li]Use interns/ex-interns just to learn about their process  \(no referral ask, just info\).
Leaning toward: Option 1 — I feel like even if they can’t refer, interns might be willing to chat or help in other ways. Just not sure how much value that really brings compared to aiming higher up the ladder.

title: DigitalOcean Internship Interview Process + Offer Received ($54/hour Remote for Summer 2025)
content:
I hope this breakdown helps anyone applying to DigitalOcean in the future! I had an amazing experience with their interview process—it was by far one of the best I’ve gone through. The entire process took only two weeks, and the timeline was incredibly smooth. Plus, no LeetCode-style questions for the internship, which might be great news for some!
💰 Compensation
[ul][li]Base Pay: $54/hour[li]Overtime Pay: $81/hour[li]Position: Remote in San Francisco, CA

📅 DigitalOcean Interview Timeline
[ul][li]Applied \(with 1 referral\): March 12, 2025[li]Invited for Recruiter Phone Screen: March 17, 2025[li]Recruiter Phone Screen: March 19, 2025[li]Final Interview \(Engineering Manager & Senior Software Engineer\): March 27, 2025[li]Offer Received: March 28, 2025 \(Recruiter called at 9 AM with the good news and sent the offer letter shortly after\)

📞 Recruiter Screen
[ul][li]Standard introduction questions, including "Can you introduce yourself?" and a few follow-ups.

💻 Final Interview
Conducted over Zoom with two interviewers: an Engineering Manager and a Senior Software Engineer.
📌 First 30 Minutes: Project Presentation
[ul][li]I presented one of my past projects.

👨‍💻 Senior Software Engineer Questions
[ol:1][li]Why did you choose this tech stack?[li]If you had to start over, what would you do differently?[li]How did you teach yourself 3D graphics and model simulation?

🛠️ Engineering Manager Questions \(mostly Behavioral Questions\)
[ol:1][li]Tell me about a time you failed and how you handled it. \(Similar to Amazon’s Leadership Principles question.\)[li]What was the timeline for your project?[li]Describe a time you missed a deadline—what did you learn from it?

⚡ The Toughest Part – Unexpected Challenge!
I wasn’t expecting this at all, and I had zero preparation for it. They asked me how I would approach a real-world problem their team is working on:
💡 "How would you approach preventing server crashes using Machine Learning?"
I had never worked with servers before, so I had no idea but I mentioned things like KPI, google search A/B testing as a way to debug this. Here’s my response:

title: Warner Bros. Discovery/Games - NetherRealm Studios Recruitment Timeline
content:
I saw a few others posting helpful information on their recruitment timelines, so I thought I'd share a general outline of how I got to my offer, as well as the questions I was asked.

The position I interviewed for was the NetherRealm Studios \(Mortal Kombat, Injustice game studio\) Software Engineering Co-op, specifically for the game engine team. I left the job posting PDF below for more details. 💲

Timeline📅

2/19 \(Morning\): Applied through LinkedIn/Workday
2/19 \(Evening\): Got an invitation for a HireVue async interview
2/21: Completed Hirevue
3/19: Invitation from recruiter for a 15 minute phone screen
3/24: Completed phone screen, received a coding OA
3/25: Submitted OA
3/31: Followed up on status, got told the hiring manager was out of office so there would be a delay
4/7: Received final round invitation
4/15: Followed up on status, received an email back saying recruiter had an "exciting update for me" and we scheduled a short phone call later that day where I verbally received the offer

Questions/Overview

HireVue / Async Interview 🎥
The HireVue was long ago so I can't remember exactly what questions there was, but they were stereotypical behavioral questions where you had about 3-4 minutes to answer each one and two attempts to record. If you chose to attempt again, it would force you to take the second attempt.

[ul][li]"Why Warner?"[li]"What programming languages do you know?"[li]"What's a project you worked on?"[li]"What's your experience with gaming?"

After the video portion, there was a 14-question multiple-choice technical quiz.

Some were easy DSA questions like..
[ul][li]"Which data structures fits this website feature best?"[li]"What's the runtime complexity of this function?"

But some were a bit more obscure
[ul][li]"What is asynchronous programming good for?"[li]"If two computers run this code at the same time, what bug could potentially arise?"

Recruiter Phone Screen 📞

The recruiter was pretty nice, and it wasn't too crazy
[ul][li]"How was your weekend?" \(I actually made conversation and talked about my weekend here\)[li]"Why Warner Bros.?"[li]"Tell me about a time you were in a leadership position"[li]"What does your dream internship look like?"

title: Ideal Approach When Applying for Multiple Positions at One Company
content:
When applying to multiple roles at the same company, it can be unclear whether submitting different tailored resumes is helpful or potentially confusing to recruiters.

Solutions:
[ol:1][li]Tailor my resume for each role to highlight the most relevant skills and experience—this shows alignment with specific job requirements.[li]Use a master resume and customize only the summary or key skills section to match each role while maintaining consistent core content.[li]Submit the same resume across all applications to avoid potential confusion if recruiters compare documents.

My suggestion: Tailor my resume for each position while maintaining consistency in your core experience—this strikes a balance between relevance and clarity for the hiring team.

title: Recruiter Tip on OA (non-technical/work style)
content:
Let's talk about these non-technical stuff on OA's. As I'm having more coaching call with all of you, I am inspired to post this OA tip to help you "think" like a ⭐Rockstar ⭐

The online assessments are kind of like a sneak peek into what the actual job would be like. They give you tasks and situations that are really similar to the stuff you'd have to do if you got hired. This helps the company see how you'd handle the real work.

🚀Below are my tips for y'all when tackling the 📣Non Technical📣 Questions:

🍭Are you able to read through information or data, and then figure out what it all means on your own?

🛑Can you take the facts and details they give you, and then use your own ability to draw conclusions?

🍭Are you able to make good decisions when you're faced with a problem or challenge?

🛑Can you handle difficult situations and look at a problem, think through the different options, and then choose the best way to solve it?

🍭Are you able to figure out the best way to plan out your work and tackle the most important stuff first?

🛑Can you look at everything you need to do, decide what's most important, and then make a solid plan for getting it all done efficiently.

🍭Are you able to solve problems in creative and effective ways?

🛑Can you can come up with unique, smart solutions to the challenges?

🍭 Are you able to communicate clearly and confidently?

title: Recruiter Tip of the Day 🚀Make yourself stand out from other candidates🚀
content:
As you are going through your interview prep, I wanted to share one question that all of you should be preparing & have well rehearsed.

Everyone should be preparing a response for "Walk me through a problem/challenge you helped to solve"

When you are approached by this question, please clearly explain the problem you are facing.

[ul][li]What did you do to gather information and understand the problem?[li]What key details or data were you missing?[li]How did you go about filling those information gaps?[li]What possible solutions did you consider, and how did you evaluate them? [li]What was your final solution and give a reason why you choose that 

Key Takeaway: 👉You got to find a way to be above your peers to make yourself stand out and to do that is to be able to tell an amazing story and showcase your problem solving abilities. Hiring Managers are looking for excellent problem solving skillsets and someone who can handle challenges with impressive analytical skills and when you are given ambiguity, you are able to handle it!

Reminder👉Never use "WE" in your response. You should take all the credit for the work, so make sure you are always using "I".

\(FYI: This post is inspired by some recent mock interview prep calls with some of you \) 🤗

title: 3/14 LeetCode Office Hours Recording
content:
In today's office hours, we went over the thought processes that should happen when solving a LeetCode problem:
[ul][li]brainstorming possible approaches[li]creating edge cases[li]implementing our code \(pseudocode in this case\)

These are valuable steps to take when solving any question and especially in a live technical interview! Feel free to watch the recording if you missed it today or join me at the next LeetCode office hour!

Recording: [https://grain.com/share/recording/38c50eea-82f4-44a5-b896-51aff08eba7a/8wwZhgSXR4cvvXrTaP38nS4Gd7SZYThq9d09xdfr](https://grain.com/share/recording/38c50eea-82f4-44a5-b896-51aff08eba7a/8wwZhgSXR4cvvXrTaP38nS4Gd7SZYThq9d09xdfr)

Corrections:
A better algorithm to use on the first TikTok problem might be one involving the identification and counting of strongly-connected-components. Union-find is usually performed on undirected graphs so there could be edge cases that may fail the recording's brainstormed approach. Regardless, the recording should exemplify how we are able to come up with potential approaches and refine them!

At the end, I mention that the time complexity for memoizing with an array would change the space complexity to O\(n^2k\), but it should still be O\(nk\). This is because we would only visit each subarray once per partition we are creating. Passing in an array for each recursion requires splicing the array which would add to the time complexity though.

title: Recruiter Resume Tip of the Day !
content:
Recruiters are trained to look for words that can tell us you have demonstrated hands on technical experience and skillset.

We like to see words such as:
Designed
Developed
Debugged\(JTAG\)
Optimized
Architected
Accelerated

Avoid: managed, facilitated, oversaw, or supervised. These words tell us you are only doing support and maintaining work and not someone who can just come onboard to hit the ground running!

HAVE A NICE DAY😀 Sending positive vibes to your job search! You got this! 💪

title: Navigating Student Program
content:
Today's office hour with many of you made me realize I need to share this post with everyone here at Accelerator to help y'all with an understanding on how to navigate through University Talent Acquisition | or also known as: Student Programs | Early Careers Pathway.

Here are the top 3 must-knows- and trust me, you all want to jump on these ASAP. Consider this your priority homework from me.

1.Sign Up for Job Alerts: Are you ready to get the scoop on the coolest internships? Make sure you're on the email lists for your dream companies. When that perfect intern spot opens up, you want to be the first to hit that “Apply Now” button! 🚀

2.Timing is Key: 🕒 Think about applying to that internship is like grabbing that limited edition or exclusive item - but there is only few lucky ones that will actually score the item. Recruiters often reject applications received after a certain date \(when applicant pool becomes to big in comparison to the actual headcount\), even if the position is still open. So, it's crucial to apply right when the job first opens.

✨please don't miss out, you need to apply as early as the position is posted ✨

3. Meet Basic Qualifications: Ensure you meet every detail of the job's basic qualifications. For example, a job specifies computer science majors, make sure you have CS listed on your resume + application. If the job description mentions specific graduation dates, make sure your resume and application align with those dates. Every detail matters!!

Last reminder would be, tailor your resume as much as you could to the ideal/preferred qualifications listed on the job description.

title: Recruiter = Biggest Ally
content:
Remember this!!

Recruiters will be your🫶 "Bestie" 🫶throughout the job search process.

Recruiters are evaluated on how quickly they can fill open roles at the company. This means they're just as invested in you succeeding through the interview process as you are! Their goal is to get you into that awesome new job as fast as possible. On top of that timing, providing you with satisfactory candidate experience is a top priority.

Are you leaning on your recruiter and building that rapport with them?

I'm telling you, recruiters should be your secret sauce and you need to keep them on your personal squad.

[ul][li]Come prepared with your perfect ice breaker to kick thing off![li]🤩Fun example was yesterday was Mario Day *3/10* and the candidate found out the recruiter was a total Super Mario fanatic and the candidate was able to kick off the call with a huge laugh and instant connection with the recruiter.[li]Forge that close bond with your recruiter, if recruiters cannot place you in their job, they can push you off to their colleagues that could use your talent![li]Be responsive when they reach out and let them know that you are excited for the role.[li]Most importantly, know recruiter's position.

SO here is my questions for all of you ⁉️

What was a fun, exciting moment where you were able to connect with a recruiter you had interacted with?

What did you experience, learn or appreciate \(or dislike\) about the interaction?

Your insightful stories could really help others navigate the hiring process so who will be brave to kick us off with sharing first?!

title: Insight: Talking to Current Employees is Amazing
content:
I've only done this once, so I'll have to update, but I just got off the phone with an employee from a company. I found them on LinkedIn awhile ago. I thought they were cool, but didn't know how to approach. I used the strategies from the networking and referral course and I'm impressed by the information I got.

They're not hiring right now \(they're not growing, so only backfilling roles right now\), but when they are, he said I could ask him about the hiring manager. He told me the job is probably likely to be in C# \(instead of Ruby\). He told me about his interview experiences, which gives me an idea of how I'd need to prepare. ...Of course, he said I could mention his name and they'd call him to confirm. \(Referral!\)

If I do this enough, I'm going to find a company that's ready to hire me for top dollar pretty quick. The information I got was just too useful. It will put me ahead of anyone that didn't have a similar conversation by a LONG shot.

It helped me a lot to have a list of questions out in front of me. I did my best to bounce between creating rapport and moving through my questions.

The greatest thing about this strategy is that it's great practice for talking to people in this context. ...Gaining some confidence.

Really cool. I had heard of the benefits of doing this and it always made sense, but I never fully realized. I just dialed myself a referral.

Thanks, Aman.

title: Tell me about a time you had to explain a technical concept to someone without a technical background
content:
I just want to make sure if my answer sounds decent or that I need to come up with a new story for this question. Down below is the general gist of it. Also sorry for the bad writing I'm just laying out ideas here.

"So at my school we have this class called introduction to programming for scientists. And this class is mostly made up of students who are in other majors like bio or chem or forensic sciences, But I guess they just have to take it for their degree requirements. So my friend was a TA for this class but for one of the weeks he couldn;t make it and asked me to cover for him. So they were reviewing "for loops" and so like I had to find a way to explain it to them to makes sense especially since they weren’t really technical people. So first what I did was use a real life analogy so say if you go to the grocery store and you are checking out and you want to scan all items in the cart until you reach the last item this is what exactly is a for loop which is doing a repeatable task until the end. Another thing was I provided an example and showed the class using a debugger how everything was working because a debugger provides more detailed information about how code is running. I also showed an example of what would happen if we did not have loop showing it's advantages. So in these tutorials basically they would have a quiz to test knowledge about the previous weeks work not for marks just for understanding and my friend told me the class ended up doing pretty well on it. This also carried over to the miderm as well. What I learned from this experience was that it helped me develop a greater deal of empath for beginner or non-technical people because sometimes when you’ve done something for so long u think it’s easy but have to understand it’s not like that for everyone. "

Bala"

title: Behavioral Interview Answer
content:
I’m preparing my response for why I want to work at Niagara Bottling and am torn between focusing on sustainability or their mission of delivering quality and affordable water. My past experiences, where I have developed apps that promote better mental health habits and analyzing health data to empower users, could tie in with either value since I am saying that I am passionate about using technology to solve real world problems. However, I’m unsure which would resonate more with the company’s priorities. Could you provide guidance on which angle might be stronger?
\(These answers will be improved more, just trying to see which angle is stronger\)

Sustainability Answer:
One of the biggest reasons I want to work for Niagara Bottling is its unwavering commitment to environmental sustainability. I’m inspired by achievements like becoming the first North American bottling plant to earn TRUE Zero Waste certification and establishing LEED Gold-certified facilities, which highlight Niagara’s leadership in reducing environmental impact. My passion lies in using technology to tackle real-world challenges, and I see immense potential to contribute to projects that advance energy efficiency and waste reduction. For example, I developed an app at LifeStages to promote mental health habits and worked at Gekko Corporation analyzing health data to empower users with AI-driven insights to improve their health. These experiences have equipped me to bring forward-thinking solutions to a company committed to tackling real-world issues.

Delivering Affordability/Quality Answer:
One of the biggest reasons I want to work for Niagara Bottling is its dedication to delivering quality, affordable water that directly benefits people and communities. I admire how Niagara achieves this through innovative practices, ensuring access to essential resources while maintaining affordability. This aligns with my passion for using technology to create solutions that improve lives. For instance, I developed an app at LifeStages to support better mental health habits and worked at Gekko Corporation analyzing health data to empower users with actionable, AI-driven insights. I’m excited about the prospect of applying my technical skills to Niagara’s mission of improving lives through innovative, high-quality solutions.

title: What's the best approach to get back on this recruiter's radar? 🤔
content:
[@Aman Manazir](obj://user/83840ae6dab145bb851045e0e0ca6c63)
Screenshot of the conversation below

A quick backstory:
Back in 2021, I attended a school networking event \(held online\) where I connected with a recruiter on LinkedIn and had a chat with her. At the time, I was aiming to secure an internship for the Summer 2022 term \(not a SWE role, by the way\). Things were going well until she sent me a message asking me to stop listing her name as a referral in job applications. Looking back, my networking skills were still a work in progress then 😂. I figured she must have been annoyed, so I gave up and started cold-applying for roles at the same company. Unfortunately, I didn’t land any of the positions I applied for that term, but I did secure an internship at another company.

Fast forward to Winter 2023: I needed another internship and decided to cold-apply to several roles at the same company again. This time, I got an interview and an offer, which was super exciting!

Now, I’m not sure if the recruiter had anything to do with the offer I received a year later, but I’ve always assumed it was pure luck.

What would be the best strategy to reconnect with her without bringing back the memory of me being "the guy who listed her as a referral without permission" for SWE roles? 😅

title: For All Asian Students Who Are Struggling: Change Your Name
content:
I wanted to address something important that may help give you an edge in the job market, especially if you have an East Asian or Indian name. In the world of tech hiring, biases are still a reality, and research has shown that applicants with certain names often face extra scrutiny or higher standards. I’m here to give you every possible advantage to make sure your skills and hard work are what truly stand out.

Here’s My Recommendation:

Only consider this approach if:
[ul][li]You’ve already put in at least 15 referrals and are still seeing low response rates \(under 10% for interviews\) despite doing everything else we teach. [li]If that’s the case, this is an advanced strategy that might be worth exploring. Otherwise, focus on foundational steps first, like optimizing your resume, networking, and applying consistently.

If Applicable, Consider Using a Different First and Last Name:

Consider using a different first and last name for job applications and on LinkedIn—something that doesn’t clearly signal ethnicity. It can be as simple as choosing a name that feels familiar in American contexts but still resonates with you. This way, recruiters and hiring managers won’t see your ethnicity right away and will be more likely to focus on your qualifications first.

Why This Can Help

[ul][li]1. Reducing Initial Bias: Names associated with East Asian or Indian backgrounds can sometimes face unconscious bias, especially as the tech field is highly competitive with many international applicants. Using a name that’s more neutral can help level the playing field, allowing your skills to shine.[li]2. Easy Implementation: Companies today are generally flexible with preferred names. Many applicants go by different names for personal or professional reasons, and hiring teams rarely question it. Just ensure that if a background check comes up, you can clarify that the name you use professionally is different from your legal name.[li]3. Add “U.S. Citizen” \(if Applicable\): If you’re a U.S. citizen, place this at the top of your resume to clarify that you’re not an international candidate. This small addition can prevent unnecessary assumptions about visa status.

title: If You Don’t Have an Internship Yet, All is Not Lost
content:
I’ve been getting this question a lot on coaching calls lately, so I wanted to address it directly here. People keep asking me, “Aman, we’re deep into the application cycle, fall is wrapping up—am I too late? Is it over for me this season?”

The answer is absolutely not.

I’ll be straightforward: you’re not done, and you’re definitely not out of options. There’s still a very good chance you can land an internship, and here’s why:

1. It’s Been Done Before: I’ve worked with many people who’ve secured internships well into spring. For example, one of my earliest students, [@Aliyan Muhammad](obj://user/b1a197612bc74fe0b20ab6ae23565a52), landed multiple offers in March 2024, long after most application cycles had finished. Personally, I also received internship offers as late as April, as well as some full-time ones.
2. Company Preferences Can Work in Your Favor: Many companies don’t want to wait months for a new hire to start. They prefer hiring a few months out—closer to summer or the intended start date. This means some companies only start recruiting now/in a few months, hoping to fill roles for spring or early summer.

So, take a deep breath. Keep applying, stay focused, and keep pushing forward. As long as you put in the work, you’re in a strong position to make it happen.

If you have any questions, drop them below, and remember—you’ve got this!

title: Understanding How to Approach Code Signals
content:
Hello Everyone,

I hope you are doing well!

After applying much of the knowledge that I gained from the accelerator, I was able to land many different OAs at various companies for this internship cycle so far \(including Meta, Uber, Roblox, etc.\).

However, many of these OAs were code signals, and unlike HackerRank, the odds are much higher. We have to do 1 easy and 3 medium questions in one hour as compared to two mediums in one hour for a hacker rank. Additionally, code signal doesn't factor code quality and commenting into the grade as HackerRank, but instead really emphasizes passing ALL test cases for each problem.

In my experience so far, I have been able to complete 2 problems successfully for each code signal, but reaching a working solution for the others in the provided time has been difficult. I either am super close and can't pass the tests due to a small bug, or for some reason, the fourth problem will just be extremely hard \(i.e. greedy or some DP problem\) that I don't know how to approach.

My question is what do you think I can do to improve on these? I have had friends state that simply using Google or other sources \(if the Code Signal is unproctored\) might be the way to go as everyone does. Then one can get to the interview stage and then these are easier to go through as you can at least explain your solution \(even if it doesn't compile\). However, I think this is just wrong and that it can end up wasting time during the OA regardless.

I have been polishing my LeetCode skills and although I have been doing this for weeks now, I don't really know if this would really matter for these Code Signals given that the grading can be very difficult and the timing is quite strange. I have read on the CS Subreddit and other places that even people who get perfect scores at times don't even reach the next round.

My point is, there are those people who grind LeetCode all day and are competitive programmers that we may be competing against again for these small number of positions. I have another chance with Meta as I got another OA from them for another SWE role, so I wanted to ask what advice you would have regarding approaching this \(especially since there is a high likelihood of another code signal appearing\).
