title: System Design Interview Resources:
content:
I recently had a system design interview \(swe intern role\) and here are the resources I used.
[ul][li][system design primer](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer) \(github repo\)[li][system design in a hurry](https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/in-a-hurry/how-to-prepare) [li][Exponent System design](https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLrtCHHeadkHp92TyPt1Fj452_VGLipJnL&si=lz57Nucsc7W_TCW2) prep youtube playlist \(super helpful because it has mock interviews and topic videos\)[li][system design case studies](https://naina0405.substack.com/p/mega-launch-105-new-system-design?r=14q3sp&utm_campaign=post&utm_medium=web&triedRedirect=true) [li][Quastor System Design Archives ](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1VAnWvukex0kuqUqTlplap6TMt7SCz5TS/view)\(pdf doc super long but has some helpful sections\)[li][freeCodeCamp system design for beginners](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m8Icp_Cid5o&list=TLPQMDYxMDIwMjQE2vnhaHQc8g&index=18&ab_channel=freeCodeCamp.org)  \(good place to start\)[li][System design Cheat sheet ](https://systemdesign.one/system-design-interview-cheatsheet/#what-to-learn-next)

One thing I've heard is that often system design interviews for interns are not going to expect you to go into as much depth/detail that some of the mock interviews and case studies. Also more often than not you won't be asked to implement an entire app/system but rather design specific a feature that is part of a larger system.

title: Conflict with Application and Referrer Message
content:
Question: The person who referred me to the company gave me the email of the recruiter who handles intern applications, but he also said that should not email him until January/February since that's when they look at resumes. However, the applications are already open. What should I do?

Sidenote: Reason he gave me the recruiters email is because they don't do referrals, they simple have the recruiter contact high priority applications.

Problem: Timing conflict between the open application period and the recommended timeframe for contacting the recruiter, potentially impacting the internship application process.

Viable solutions:
[ol:1][li] Submit your application now and set a reminder to follow up with the recruiter in January/February.[li] Send a brief, polite email to the recruiter now, explaining your situation and asking for guidance on the best approach. [li] Apply now and include a note in your application stating your intention to follow up with the recruiter in January/February.

Suggestion: Submit your application now and set a reminder to follow up with the recruiter in January/February.

title: Common Referral Objections + How To Overcome
content:
Hey everyone — I'm going to cover this topic in-depth in a referral module that's coming out in 1-2 weeks, but for now, here's the most common referral objections you'll hear from people and how to overcome them.

Remember -- there is no loss if they dislike you. You're not trying to be their friend — you just need to get a referral from them, so make yourself push a bit.

[ul][li]“The referral doesn’t do much at my company”

“Totally understand — I expect that at big companies like yours a lot of people get referrals, so it might not make a huge difference. But it can’t hurt, right? I get that in the end it might not change much, but in the off chance that it does, would you be able to submit one for me? It would really really help out!”

[ul][li]“I don’t know what our referral process is / I haven’t heard much about that, I’ll have to look into it.”

“Totally understand, makes complete sense, and I appreciate that. When do you think you’ll be able to find out about the referral process? Is there someone you’ll have to ask?”

Gets more commitment from them — if they verbally say they will refer you, it’s unlikely that they just ghost or don’t later on.

[ul][li]“Sorry, at our company, we only really refer people who we work with closely.”

This one is really unlikely, and the hardest one to overcome because it’s a straight up rejection — I just want to put it here to get it on your radar.

“Of course, that makes complete sense, and I appreciate the time you took out to get on this call and help me with the interview process and tell me about your journey. Would it be possible to….”

Use their response to get contact at company.

[ul][li]“My team doesn’t hire interns/new grads/your role.”

“Makes complete sense, do you know of any other people who have worked with interns/new grads/role at all? Even if you’ve just heard of them at the company, if you could connect me with that person that would be extremely helpful — just to make sure my resume gets seen, you know how these applications go.

title: Weekly Routine To Land FIRST Paid Internship:
content:
\(OP\) Aman Manazir - Weekly Routine To Land FIRST Paid Internship:
[ol:1][li]Find 10 new companies that have open internships that are not name brand / small name brand that you qualify for[li]Send out 10-15 networking connection requests to people who work at EACH of those companies[li]Find people with similar age, early in career, similar University \(Oregon, Arkansas\).[li]Wait 3-5 days and get on a call with them to get referral + interview info + contact with hiring manager[li]If no response, send out 10 more for that company.[li]After 6-7 days total, apply[li]Repeat Next Week[li]10 more companies + entire process week by week[li]Even if you already applied, and they respond late, get the referral anyway.[li]Ask for referral after you applied, if they say no, then get the hiring manager / recruiter email so your resume gets seen.[li]Even if the company doesn’t have an internship open YET, still get the referral + one other contact \(phone number, email\)[li]You need referral with ideally 1 software engineer + 1 software engineering manager - don’t need more.[li]REPEAT

This approach is almost identical if you’re going for your second or third internship as well, but just a different selection of companies.

title: LinkedIn Connection Request Template (Alumni)
content:
Here’s a LinkedIn connection request template for an alumni:
“Hey \[first name\], it’s nice to meet you! I’m \[first name\] — a current computer science student at \[your University\]. I noticed that you’re an alumni and also work at \[company name\]. That’s amazing!

I’m very interested in \[aspect 1 of their company that connects with your background\] as I’ve done extensive work in \[that area\] as well through \[experience\].

I’d love to connect with you and potentially learn more about your experience! Thank you so much!

Please modify the above to fit your unique circumstance — also, if you get an acceptance/reply, please send those in this channel \(your message and their reply\) — we want to adapt this template to be as high converting as possible.

As a goal, all of you should aim to grow your LinkedIn to 500+ high quality connections — I’d advise sending off 5-10 personalized connections per day, and expecting about 1/3-1/2 to convert \(might adapt over time\). Within 4-6 months you’ll hit this mark.

In addition, you need to connect with every single person you’ve ever met. Friends, family, professors, literally everyone — these will convert at a much higher rate than cold profiles. Go through your phone contacts, text messages, Instagram followers, and connect with all of them.

Once you build this network, it’ll be a gold mine. You’ll be able to search a company name, see that you have 1-3 connections working there, and then direct message for an information interview + referral.

Caveat — don’t spam non-personalized non-high quality connection requests. Only connect with people you already know or you have a good reason to connect with them.

title: LinkedIn Premium
content:
It looks like LinkedIn has put a 5 personalized connection request limit per month to non-Premium members, which is unfortunate. Because of this, I’d recommend upgrading to LinkedIn premium. You can send up to 100 personalized connections per week which is more than enough.

In addition, $30/month seems expensive, but if you consider the ROI it’s definitely worth it.

You can also use it for a few months until you get your internship/job and then cancel.

title: Resources for Writing Emails
content:
\(OP\) Aman Manazir: Here’s a really great resource for learning how to write cold emails — I’d advise all of you skim through this and use it in your cold messages/emailing

In addition, I would follow a principle called The Fortune is in the Follow-Up — use the script in there to follow up with pretty much everyone who doesn’t respond to your email. After 3-4 days follow up, and then every week for 5-10 weeks straight.

Also, if you guys create a nice simple email footer, it can also help response rates — goal is to seem as friendly and normal as possible

content:
\(OP\) Navya Ramakrishnan: Hey Aman, I just had a quick question - looks like Google SWE internship application is due tomorrow, which is a pretty tight deadline - for this would you just recommend prioritizing getting the application done rather than seeing if there's any networking / referral I could get for it in 24 hours? Aman: Hi Navya, so my thoughts on this are to try to get a referral in the next 24h, and if you can’t land one, then apply anyway.
[ul][li]When do the applications close?[li]You should find 8-10 people on LinkedIn who are Harvard alumni, similar age range/ethnicity, at Google, and then send them a connection request with the provided template
[ul][li]You’ll want to mention early that you’re also at Harvard \(introduce yourself with major + school\), and then mention something particular about their experience/background that you find interesting[li]Finally say that you’re really interested in what Google is like and you’d love to eventually work there
[ul][li]You want to ask them to hop on a short 15 min call to learn more about them/their background[li]Another aspect to this is that I think you should be sending out a handful of connection requests every day to qualified people at companies you’re interested in \(provided you’ve fixed your LinkedIn\) 

Advice for sending out connection requests:
[ul][li]Don’t spam people, make your request tailored/custom to them[li]Setting up frequent information interviews will put you very far ahead, even if a position isn’t open. It gives you a connection, and this game is about building a network that you can tap later on[li]Let’s say I connect with someone at Amazon — then Amazon opens up a few weeks later — I now have an instant referral

title: Q&A: CodeSignal
content:
\(OP\) Krishiv Gubba: Aman, I've received an OA in the form of a codesignal assessment. Do you have any pointers regarding this?
Do you know which topics are heavily tested?

Aman Manazir: Here’s my advice:
[ul][li]Watch CodeSignal Videos: Look up recent videos on CodeSignal to understand the platform and any updates.

[ul][li]Understand the Format: There are usually four questions. The first two are easier, while the third and fourth are more challenging. Focus on math, dynamic programming, arrays, strings, and greedy algorithms, as these topics are more common than graphs and trees.

[ul][li]Practice Assessments: Take several CodeSignal practice assessments to familiarize yourself with the format and question types.

[ul][li]Work Linearly: Don’t skip the first problem to tackle later ones. Work through the questions in order and aim to get each one right, as this will contribute to your overall score.

[ul][li]Stay Updated: Since there might be updates, watching videos can give you the latest tips and tricks.

title: Q&A Studying Neetcode
content:
\(OP\) Jayanth Srinivas: Hey Aman, I have completed all the Pareto Problem Set questions. Do I start solving Neetcode 150 questions next or are there any other specific list of questions that I should start solving? Or I should revisit and revise all the problems in the Pareto list again?

Aman Manazir: I would say go through the NeetCode 150 now, but maybe focus on the Pareto topics, and go in a linear order trying to understand everything to the best of your ability.

Jayanth Srinivas: Understood. And one more thing, I wanted to take some time to focus on studying the patterns to solve the Pareto topic questions. Do you think it is a good idea to exclusively study the recurring patterns to identify the tricks to solve a new question? Or do you think it is a waste of time and I am better if solving more questions from Neetcode?

Aman Manazir: I would say spend some time studying the patterns after you solve the problem \(maybe 1h\), and then move forward and practice more of the same topic on NeetCode.

title: Q&A: System Design in Python
Coding Interview Structure Advice
content:
OP - Jason Sun

Hi guys, I got this coding Interview structure from a career meeting with a alumni working in meta. I think it would be very useful and want to share it here:
[ol:1][li]Investigate: Ask clarifying questions. Define the input/outputs. Suggest constraints. Discuss obvious edge cases.[li]Brute-force it: Suggest the obvious answer. Solve as if solving manually. Explain and code-comment your solution. Draw whiteboard diagrams if available.[li]Calculate Complexity: How much time does each line take? What's the O\(n\)? How much space is needed?[li]Optimize: Pinpoint the heaviest operations. Eliminate duplicated effort. Use data structures to speed up saving/retrieval. Write down the new time and space complexity.[li]Code: Code alongside your comments. Write simple, readable, and maintainable code. Mention edge cases.[li]Test and Verify: List and check all possible edge cases. Walk through the code with a sample input to verity output.
